s01.slug: THURSDAY · 12:15 PM · ANACAPA COMMONS — THE WINDOW TABLE
body: It is the first dry Thursday since the storms, and the window table in the Commons has the sun on it end to end, a long yellow slab of January, the first in two weeks that anyone could sit in. The glass is warm enough to lean on. Out on the lawn the bike racks are steaming, and a girl in a Serra Hall sweatshirt has carried an entire mattress pad outdoors to dry and stands over it with her arms folded.

Jack comes straight from Oceanography, where Skye spent the hour in the back row under the exit sign and left at the bell for a hair appointment in Montecito that Corinne booked, and he is hungry. Kevin is there first. His tray is lined up with the edge of the table, his BlackBerry lies face down beside the napkins, and next to a plate of eggs he hasn’t touched are two index cards: one soft at the corners from a week in a shirt pocket, one new and white, filled to the margins in his small careful letters.

body.text: “You asked me to hold you to something,” Kevin says, before Jack has set down his tray. “I’m holding.” He moves the second chair out from the table with his foot.
body.else: Kevin asked him in the hall last night: lunch, Thursday, the window table, *I have a list*. Now, before Jack has set down his tray, he moves the second chair out from the table with his foot.

body: By the cereal bar the Louisiana table has hung a gold ribbon on the milk dispenser and is on its third *Who dat?* since Jack came in, ten days out from Miami, with the waffle line answering. Jack’s eyes stay on Kevin’s cards. The cereal bar is a cereal bar.
“Before the list,” Kevin says, and lays his fork in the groove of the tray. “Laney told Margot. Margot told me. I asked her not to, and she said it was a public-health matter.”

body.text: “I’m not taking a side. I don’t have the information and I don’t want it.” He turns the new card face down. “Just — you were both on my list for the van. I’d like to never have to make that list again.”
body.else: “Evan said the dog shook.” He turns the new card face down. “I’m a dog person. That’s all I’ve got.”

body: “It’s done, Kev.”

Kevin looks at him across the two cards. He turns the new one face up again and picks up his fork. Jack is hungry in a plain, uncomplicated way, and the eggs are good: the Commons runs breakfast all day on Thursdays, for reasons lost to history, and somebody in the back has finally learned what butter is for.

Margot comes by the window table with a hot water and one piece of dry toast, in the black she wears for grief and for everything else, and does not slow down to deliver it. “Salinger’s dead. Ninety-one. New Hampshire.” She tips the toast toward the register, where a girl in a Lit sweatshirt has her face in a bagel. “The *Times* had the obituary ready, which tells you something about the *Times*.”
“Was he Catholic?” Kevin asks.
“He was everything for about a year each.” She sets a napkin at the Lit girl’s elbow without breaking stride and carries the rest of her breakfast to a table by herself, with her back to the room.
“That’s her version of a sympathy card,” Kevin says, low, of the napkin. “She’ll say it was sanitation.”
Doug goes by with two trays and a hash brown in his mouth, takes in the cards over Kevin’s shoulder, and says “Dude” with feeling. “Just tell her you like her violin.”
“I do like her violin,” Kevin says. “It’s item one.”
“Then you’re done,” Doug says, and carries his trays off to a table in the sun with a man’s total confidence, and Kevin watches him go. “He’s right,” he says. “It’s the worst thing about him.”
“So,” Kevin says, and taps the new card, and Jack watches him become an attending. “Hour four. Presentation of the problem.”

He lays it out in order of severity. The first hour of any encounter is the history and physical; hours two and three are the procedure; hour four is recovery, and he has never been handed a script for recovery. The Walk van was six hours and Clare slept five of them, which is not a problem but is data. Javi has invited him to a Niners game in the fall, with the family, an offer Kevin describes as a standing order: nine hours door to door, the tailgate and the game and the drive back down 280, and somewhere in the third quarter, with four brothers on one side of him and the thermos empty on the other, there is an hour when no one is being introduced to anyone and the prepared material has run out. “One through three, I’m great,” he says. “I have the handshake.”
“The long normal one.”

“It’s a long normal one,” Kevin says, with dignity, “and I’ve worked on it.” He holds out his hand across the table to prove it, and Jack takes it: three seconds, eye contact, no pump. It comes back to Jack feeling reviewed.
“Nine out of ten,” Jack says. “Lose the left hand on the elbow. That’s a county commissioner.”
“It’s *warm*.”
“It’s a county commissioner.” Kevin takes his left hand off his own elbow and looks at it.
Kevin turns the new card around and slides it over, and Jack reads it with a forkful of egg held in the air.

body.title: Index card, in Kevin’s hand
body.text:
THINGS TO SAY AT HOUR FOUR

1. Her violin (chin rest? NOT the sound)
2. Her brothers: four. Names, in order (J, L, N, T)
3. The Walk — how are her knees
4. “Do you like the 9:30 or is it a family thing”
5. Niners, 9–7 last year (verify)
6. The measure with which you measure (today’s Gospel — too much?)
Under the Gospel, one more line has been crossed out once and written over in the same small letters: *Thank Skye (via Jack).*

body: “Why not the sound?” Jack asks, at the first line.

“Because I can’t tell a good one from a bad one,” Kevin says, “and she knows it. She told me hers was her grandfather’s, a Czech violin, and I said *wow*, and she said, *You don’t know anything about violins*, and I said *No*.” He looks happy. “It was the best moment of the Walk.”
“Eight and eight,” Jack says, and taps the fifth line. “Last year. The Niners. They were eight and eight.”
Kevin looks at the line. “Clare would know that.”
“Clare would know that.”

He crosses out *9–7* with one ruled stroke, writes *8–8* over it, and says, with feeling, “This is why I need a second reader.” He taps the sixth line. “The Gospel today is the lamp on the lampstand, and the measure you give being the measure you get. I went to Mass this morning. It’s Aquinas’s feast, and it was in my head. Too much?”
“For a Niners game?”
“For a Niners game with her *brothers*.”
“Too much.”
“I knew it,” Kevin says, happier than he has been all lunch, and does not cross it out. He uncaps the pen. “Be honest. Where does it fall over?”

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side.

choices.text: *Tell him what hour four is actually like.*
choices.key: At the window table Kevin asked what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. You told him what it’s actually like. He wrote it down.
response: Jack puts the fork down. It turns out there is an hour-four speech in him that he hasn’t been told about, and it comes up whole.

“You stop listening for your turn,” he says. “That’s first. You’ve been holding your next sentence for three hours, and somewhere in there you notice you dropped it, and you’re just listening, and what she’s saying is better than what you had. Then you find out you’ve been arguing for an hour about a book you can’t stand, and you’d pick it up again tomorrow to keep going. And you look at the clock, and it’s later than you thought, and all you want is for the drive home to be longer.” He hears himself stop. “That’s hour four, Kev. You want the drive to be longer.”

Kevin has been writing it down. Word for word, in the small careful letters, across the white card at the speed of Jack’s voice, and somewhere around *the drive* the pen quits and rests on the paper. He reads it back to himself once, carefully, like a label.
“Okay,” he says, brightly. “Seven out of ten pre-meds would have said *comfortable silence*. I was going to say *comfortable silence*.”
“It’s a good answer, *comfortable silence*.”
“It’s the answer of a man with a list,” Kevin says.
He caps the pen, folds the white card once, and slides it into his shirt pocket behind the old one.

choices.text: *Be Clare. Be a better Clare than Clare.*
choices.key: At the window table you played Clare for Kevin — badly, then well — so he could practice hour four on you.
response: “Give me your Niners cap,” Jack says.
Kevin has it in his backpack, folded in thirds like a flag. Jack puts it on backward and becomes Clare Dominguez.

He does her badly first. His Clare has a voice from somewhere between a game-show contestant and Margot, and she holds an invisible violin like a cello and saws at it from the elbow, and Kevin, wounded, says, “She doesn’t do the elbow,” and Jack drops an octave, hunches over an invisible playbook, and says, “Third and long, Kevin. What’s the formation?”
“Pray?” Kevin says.

Jack, as Clare, lowers the playbook and only looks at him, patient, with ten thousand dinners in it, until Kevin says, “It’s a nickel package, I think, they’ll have a safety in the box —” and runs down, because the girl across the table has started to smile at him and is not being unkind about it.
“You don’t have to ask about my brothers, Kevin,” Clare says, low and amused and not doing any elbow at all. “They’re going to ask about you. Javi already has a folder.”
Kevin laughs, a real one, and forgets the bit entirely and answers her. “I said *Honorable, sir*.”
“You did.”
“He told me not to call him sir.”
“He likes you.”
“Do you think —” Kevin stops. He takes the cap off Jack’s head by the bill and holds it in both hands. “Out of character. What are you supposed to feel at hour four? Actually.”

Jack gives it to him out of character too, shorter and with less on it. “That you’ve stopped keeping score. That you’d rather be bored with her than entertained by anybody else, and you aren’t bored. That you want the drive to be longer.”

Kevin writes it on the back of the white card, and his pen slows on the last line and writes it smaller than the rest. Then he turns the old card face up, the one with *Thurs. — hr 4* copied onto it in the small careful letters, and puts a check mark after it. “That was the ask,” he says, and sets the cap on his own head, forward, as God intended.

response: “That’s the list,” Kevin says, and looks at his watch. “So I have fifty-eight minutes and twenty seconds I haven’t planned.”

He turns the white card over. At the bottom of the back a line has been ruled in pen, and nothing is written on it. “This one I couldn’t write.” He is looking at the ruled line. “What are you supposed to feel? At hour four. I have the questions. No one told me what it’s supposed to be.”

s02.slug: THURSDAY · 3:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE TIE
body: The iron has been going ten minutes. 412 does not own an ironing board and Theo has declined to believe in that, so the shirt is laid across a towel on the lid of Jack’s footlocker, and Theo irons as he does everything he was never taught, at a speed that implies mastery, back and forth over the same collar. On the windowsill his speaker is playing a record from 1982 on which a saxophone sounds like money.

There is no seminar. Hale is in New York today, according to the Philosophy Department’s e-mail, to which Theo has subscribed himself along with every other list the department keeps (“the last epistolary novel in print”), and he has translated the notice aloud twice already: “*On a matter of public disputation* means being rude to a churchman on a stage, for money.” Jack has the afternoon, and Gloria has given him the night off for it, with a look. He has a suit to be pinned into.

It is the only one of Theo’s suits that Jack’s shoulders will go into, a charcoal, and it goes on over them. Below the belt it is Theo’s. Theo is four inches taller and is kneeling at Jack’s ankles with two of Priya’s safety pins, taken from a laminated EMERGENCIES envelope on her door in a transaction Priya has not yet been informed of.
“Hold still,” he says. “You are a hem in motion.”
“Is this an emergency?”
“Look at your trousers.” On the nightstand Hollis presides from his teacup, retired with honors.
“How do I walk in these?”
“Like you own the trousers,” Theo says, through the second pin. “They’ll believe you.”
When the hem is done he does the shoes, Jack’s own black ones from the Mooney spring formal. 412 has no brush, so he works the polish in with a sock pulled over his fist, and the sock is Jack’s.
The RAZR goes off on the desk at 3:31.

body.text: wear the tie he picks. not the one you like. i will explain nothing

body: “Read it again,” says Theo from the floor, so Jack does, and Theo nods at the shoe. “*Not the one you like.* I have known that girl a very long time, and I want it noted that she has never once been wrong about a tie.”
“It’s a fundraiser in the Palisades,” Jack says. “That’s all I’ve got. Her publicist says it’s civic.”

“Everything in Los Angeles is civic, Costigan. It’s how they get the parking.” Theo gets up off his knees, takes a navy silk off the closet door, and goes to the full-length mirror, where he knots it on himself for the lesson. “There are three honest knots,” he says. “The four-in-hand is for the young and the guilty. It’s lopsided, it’s loose, it looks like you got dressed in a moving car, and the world forgives you. The Windsor is for men who have been photographed. A half-Windsor is a *commitment*, Costigan. Like a coat.”
“And the fourth knot?”

“There isn’t a fourth knot. There are men who want to be asked about their knot.” The navy goes over, under, through. “Lapels next. The lapel is the only part of a jacket with a point of view. Pocket square: no. A pocket square is a cry for help in silk.” He reaches across and settles Jack’s lapel with a thumb. “You look like a man someone would vouch for, Costigan. It’s a dreadful risk.”

In the mirror, over Theo’s shoulder, the open door of 412 shows a slice of the hall, and a pink BlackBerry goes across it at hip height and stops. Laney is above it in a quilted vest and full makeup, one hand on the doorframe, her mouth open on the beginning of something. It lasts a second. Theo’s hands stop on the knot. The pink BlackBerry goes on down the hall toward the stairs, and the slice of hall is only a hall. Jack, trousers pinned, is looking at his own cuff.

body.text: It takes Theo a moment to find the knot again. When he has it up to his collar he says it to the knot: “You were good at it. Wednesday. That’s what I didn’t like.”
“Pick a tie,” Jack says.
Theo lets it be picked. He slides the navy off over his head, still knotted, and drops it on the bed.

Theo knots and unknots the navy twice more and says nothing about Wednesday, and the nothing is the loudest thing in 412. “Pick a tie,” he says. He slides it off over his head, still knotted, and drops it on the bed.

body: Beside it on the bedspread lie the two candidates. Theo’s is a dark green knit that, he says, *says I read*. The other is the red silk Ma bought at the Southern Park Mall for Christmas Mass, the best thing Jack owns, worn exactly once.

choices.text: *Hold up the one you like.*
response: Jack holds up the red one.
Theo takes it by the tail and studies it at arm’s length. “That tie is a confession, Costigan. Your mother bought it for a Christmas Mass in Ohio. It wants to go home.”
“It’s a good tie.”
“It’s a great tie for a boy in a pew. Tonight you’re a boy in a room.” He hangs it back on the closet door and smooths it straight, and the green goes on.

He ties it on Jack himself, from behind, both of them facing the mirror, a half-Windsor, quick and tight, the saxophone sliding along somewhere in the room. He turns Jack by the shoulders to see the result.
“Don’t agree with anyone,” he says.

choices.text: “You pick. She said you’d know.”
response: Theo doesn’t look at either tie. “That is either the nicest thing you’ve ever said to me or a delegation of authority,” he says. “Either way I accept the commission.” He lifts the green off the bedspread, stands Jack in front of the mirror, and ties it on him himself, a half-Windsor, very fast, and for once doesn’t narrate it. The only sounds in 412 are the saxophone and the silk being drawn up through itself. He draws the knot up to a finger’s width from the collar button and sets it with his thumbs. “Snug enough to feel,” he says. “Loose enough to leave.” He steps back.
“Don’t agree with anyone, Costigan,” he says, gently, and hangs the red one back on the closet door, where it can wait.

choices.text: *Let him do the whole speech.*
response: “Go ahead,” Jack says, and sits on the edge of the bed with his hands between his knees, and Theo gives him all of it.

There are the dimples. There is the gorge of a lapel, demonstrated on Jack’s own jacket with a finger, and the long sad history of the Duke of Windsor, wrong in two particulars and delivered flawlessly, and a digression on why no man who has ever worn a tie clip has had a happy ending. Jack sits through all of it, because the end is where Theo is happiest, and the clock on the RAZR can do what it likes.

By the time the green is on, a half-Windsor, tight and symmetrical, the RAZR says 4:38. Theo turns Jack to the mirror by the shoulders. “Don’t agree with anyone,” he says. Two minutes later a horn goes twice down at the curb, and Theo’s hands come off Jack’s shoulders.

s02a.slug: THURSDAY · 4:40 PM · US-101 SOUTH → PACIFIC COAST HIGHWAY — THE SAAB, TOP UP
body: By the Rincon the sun is down level with the soft top, coming in flat off the water under the visor, and it lays a stripe of gold across the dash and the backs of Skye’s hands at the top of the wheel. Out past the point the surfers sit their boards in a loose row, waiting on a set. The iPod rides on its cord in the cup holder, and a boy on it is singing over cheap bright guitars, delighted with everything.

At the curb in front of Delgado she took him in with one look, from the knot of Theo’s half-Windsor down to the safety pins at his cuffs, and said nothing at all, and pulled out. She has saved it for the Rincon.
“Ted dressed you,” she says.
“How do you know?”
“Only Ted ties a half-Windsor on a Thursday.”

She’s in green herself, a dark knit dress with long sleeves and very little skirt, a shade off the tie — close enough that anybody who sees the two of them together tonight will assume they planned it. He has been waiting since half past three for the explanation. She told him she would explain nothing, and so far she is a woman of her word.

Past Ventura she thumbs the iPod off and the radio on, for the traffic, and gets the news instead: Salinger, dead at ninety-one in New Hampshire, the family announcing it today. Jack heard it at lunch, from Margot, with footnotes. Skye turns the man on the radio down to a murmur.

“Three agents,” she says. “Three auditions. Three different agents told me to read that book for three different sad-girl parts, like it was a vitamin. So I read it three times.” She checks her mirror and goes around a cement truck. “I hated him every time. He’s the only boy in literature who gets to hate everybody and still be the nice one.”
“He doesn’t hate everybody.”
“Name somebody.”
“Phoebe.”
“His little sister. She’s a sidekick. She’s there so he has somebody to be adorable at.”
“The ducks.”
“Everybody loves ducks.” She takes a hand off the wheel to wave all ducks away. “Ducks are the cheapest laugh in the business. Put a duck in a scene and I don’t care how bad the scene is.”

“His brother died,” Jack says. “Allie. Leukemia. The night it happened Holden slept in the garage and broke every window in it with his fist. He was thirteen. His hand still hurts when it rains.” The Santa Clara goes by under the bridge, wide and running brown after last week’s storms, the willows along it standing in the water to their knees. “You don’t do that because you hate everybody.”
She drives. Her thumb taps the wheel, not to anything on the radio. She reaches over and turns the radio the rest of the way off.
“Fine,” she says. “He’s grieving. He’s still the worst.” She puts the blinker on for Las Posas. “If he’d had you in the car he’d have been explained to himself by Camarillo.”
At the light at the bottom of the ramp she picks the white iPhone up off her lap and reads Corinne off it in Corinne’s vowels, every one of them ironed.
“*Arrive seven. Photographer at the valet. One hour. Civic.*” She says *civic* again, slower, like the name of a perfume. “She bills by the word.”
“Whose house?”
“Gil Abernathy’s. He runs the TV side of Meridian. He cries at his own pilots.” The light changes, and she drops the phone in the door pocket.

body.text: “And you owe me four minutes,” she says. “Like Studio City. Four minutes where nobody’s looking at me. I’m cashing them in a room full of donors.”
body.else: “You stand on my left,” she says, “half a step back. Like you’re carrying my bag and you’re proud of it.” He asks what’s in the bag. “Everything,” she says. “Act like it.”

body: Las Posas runs out through the strawberry fields to the sea, and PCH comes down along the Navy’s fence to Point Mugu, where the road goes through a notch somebody blasted out of the mountain years ago and leaves the big rock standing on the ocean side, out in the surf, with the last of the light going off the water behind it. After that it’s Malibu in the blue dark — lamps on in the houses on the sand, the water a paler black than the hills — and then the first lights coming on up in the canyons.
He tells her about the three honest knots.
“Ted has three honest knots and eleven coats. I’ve seen the closet.” She shakes her head at the road. “They’re all still auditioning.”
At a light by the pier she reaches over and moves his knot a hair to the left, and looks at it, and moves it back.

It’s full dark by the light at Sunset. The ocean is off to the right, heard more than seen, and on the near corner there’s a kiosk that used to belong to a gas station, the pumps long gone and the islands painted over, with a hand-lettered menu in the window and a heat lamp already on over two stools outside. The lamp makes a little orange room in the dark, about the size of a parking space, empty yet.

Skye has both hands at the top of the wheel, and her lips are moving. He doesn’t have to hear it; he knows the shape of it by now, Nonna’s prayer in Skye’s California — *since I can’t right now*, *as if You were already there* — said under her breath to a red light on the Pacific Coast Highway, and he watches her mouth do it and wants to marry the red light.

It goes green. She swings left, up Sunset, and the heat lamp slides away behind them in the mirror, and the road starts to climb into the hills, the houses stepping back from it behind hedges and gates. A block up, late, she finishes.
“Amen,” she says.
“Amen,” Jack says.

s03.slug: THURSDAY · 7:05 PM · THE PALISADES — A HOUSE ABOVE THE VILLAGE
body: The photographer is a heavy man in a fleece vest at the foot of the front steps, with a flash the size of a lunch box, and he gets them coming up out of the motor court: Skye’s hand through Jack’s arm, her face turned up to him laughing at nothing, and Jack in a borrowed suit, looking like a man in a borrowed suit, because he is. The flash leaves a pale blot floating on everything for the next twenty feet.
Corinne is just inside, at the near end of the bar, with her BlackBerry and a Diet Coke in a highball glass. She doesn’t look up. “Seven-oh-two,” she says, and types it.

The house is glass on three sides. To the east the city lies lit to the edge of the world, Santa Monica and Westwood and the towers downtown and the grid going on past them into a brown glow at the bottom of the sky. To the west there’s nothing at all, a black the windows give the room back in — every lamp twice, every guest twice — and somewhere down in it, the ocean.

Over the stairs to the lower floor somebody has hung a long blue banner with a senator’s name on it in white, and *2010*. On every tray that comes by, under the crab cakes and the little paper cones of tuna, there’s a cream card with a number to call and boxes to tick — $250, $1,000, $2,400, the most the law lets one person give. It’s an early fundraiser for Barbara Boxer, who is running for a fourth term. She isn’t here. It’s January, and a Thursday, and this is the kind of room a candidate comes to in October.
Jack takes a card off a tray, reads it, and puts it back where it was.

Gil Abernathy is a big, soft-spoken man with a tan he keeps up like a lawn. He calls Skye *kiddo* and holds her out at arm’s length to look at her, and shakes Jack’s hand with both of his, and says any friend of hers. His wife Janine has a silver bob and a real handshake, and asks Jack where he’s from, and when he says Youngstown she says, “Oh, *Ohio*,” warmly, and asks if it’s snowing there now.

Early on, a showrunner named Nate Shulman stands two steps up the staircase under the banner with a glass of red and says a few words. His show is about two detectives and a dog, and the dog tested best. “She’s running for a fourth term,” he says, “and I would like her to get it. I would also like *Harbor Division* to get a fourth season, and only one of those is up to the people in this room.” He finds the host with his glass. “Gil. I’m looking at you.” Gil laughs loudest, and everybody laughs with him, and Nate comes down off the stairs to a scatter of applause, pleased and a little embarrassed.

Skye works the room, and she is wonderful at it. She has the bartender’s name by her second club soda — he’s an actor too, a callback Tuesday for a cereal — and asks after the callback by her third. She gets Gil to tell the one about the network chairman and the koi pond. She remembers Janine’s daughter’s name, and the name of Janine’s daughter’s horse. Jack stands at her elbow and loves watching her be good at a thing. He counts the laughs as they go by: the big one for Gil is the job, and the ones for the donors are the job, and the one that gets out of her when the bartender does his cereal line for her, deadpan, with a bar spoon, isn’t.
A woman from the network takes her off his arm for a minute, and Jack ends up beside the shrimp.

Marla Kessler finds him there. She’s sixty or close to it, and she tells him in the first minute that she’s married to one of Nate’s writers and that before that she did legal aid in Fresno. She talks to him the way everyone in this house is going to talk to him all night, like a man who came in on Skye’s arm and so must be on her side of it.

“The Stupak people,” she says. “They passed it on a Saturday night in November and went home and slept fine. You know who doesn’t sleep fine? A girl waiting tables in Fresno with no insurance and no car and a bad month. I had clients like her for eleven years.” She looks at her wine. “I had a friend like her before that. She was nineteen. It was before. She didn’t go to a doctor, because there wasn’t one to go to.” She drinks. “So you’ll forgive me if I don’t find the man *principled*.”
Jack nods. He has an answer, and her friend is in it too. He eats the shrimp instead.

Glenn Sato produces something with helicopters in it. He comes by with a crab cake on a cocktail napkin and picks up where Marla left off. “Here’s what kills me,” he says. “Sixty is gone. Massachusetts took it. And the whole bill — thirty million people who can’t see a doctor — is hostage to the bishops. A handful of men in red hats, holding thirty million people over one line.” It’s a good line, and it comes out sounding like it’s been said before, somewhere with better light.
“Most of them wear purple, technically,” Jack says. “The red’s for cardinals.”

It doesn’t land. Glenn looks at him with honest puzzlement, and Jack takes a sip of his club soda, and Glenn goes back to his crab cake. By the windows a man is telling a woman that Bernanke got his seventy, thank God, and the woman says thank God is a strong word.
Five days ago he walked Market Street and the Embarcadero behind a banner, in sneakers. He can feel it in his shoes.

Waiters come through with trays of champagne, and somebody puts a flute in Jack’s hand. Gil goes up three steps under the banner and taps his glass with his wedding ring, and the room turns toward him, and the room in the black windows turns too. Across it, by the bar, Skye has a glass up already, saying something to the bartender that makes him laugh.
Gil keeps it short. He raises his glass.
“To a woman’s right to choose,” he says, “and the votes to protect it.”
Every glass in the room goes up, and every glass in the windows goes up with it.

choices.text: *Hold it at your side.*
response: He doesn’t raise it. The champagne stays down by his pocket, going quietly flat, while the room drinks.

A waiter with an empty tray notices — a glance at the glass, a glance at him — and moves on. No one else does. Jack puts the polite face back on, the one for funerals and other people’s parishes, and wears it.

choices.text: *Raise it halfway. Don’t drink.*
response: The glass goes up as far as his shoulder and comes back down full. Across the room Janine Abernathy catches his eye over the rim of hers and smiles at him, and he smiles back.
It costs nothing, and it isn’t free. He keeps the polite face on and sets the full flute on a passing tray, carefully, so it won’t spill.

choices.text: *Find something urgent to do with a shrimp.*
response: For the length of the toast he is extremely interested in cocktail sauce. He dips. He weighs the depth of the dip. He dips again, with real care, the flute parked on the tablecloth beside the ice.
Glenn Sato catches him at it and raises his eyebrows at him, one comedian to another, as if it’s a bit. Jack lets him think so, and keeps the polite face on, with sauce on his thumb.

s04.slug: THURSDAY · 7:30 PM · THE PALISADES — THE TERRACE
body: The terrace runs the length of the west side, and it’s cold out here, January cold, the hills giving their day back to the sky. Two tall propane heaters hiss at either end over empty chairs. Jack stands at the rail and looks out at where the ocean is. He can’t see it. He can see Sunset winding down toward it in a string of streetlights, and the place where the lights stop.

He isn’t angry with her. He checks, like a man patting his pockets for his keys, and it isn’t there. She never said what tonight was for, and he never asked, and he’s nearly sure it never crossed her mind that anybody would need telling; in every room she has ever worked, nobody would. Pop would have walked out at the banner. Pop would have eaten the shrimp first.

She must have seen it from across the room; she reads a room the way he reads a book. The glass door slides behind him, and her heels come across the stone, and she’s at the rail beside him with her club soda.

body.text: “You raised your glass halfway,” she says. “I’ve never seen anybody look so Catholic holding a drink.”
“You’ve been holding that shrimp for six minutes,” she says. “It’s dead, Youngstown. Let it go.”
“You didn’t drink to it,” she says. “I watched you not.”

body: She bumps him with her hip. “What’s up, Youngstown? You’re doing your polite face.” She tips her head at him, smiling. “You’ve only got the one.”
“Nothing,” he says. “It’s a nice house.” He nods at the dark, the lights, the heaters. “Gil says you can see Catalina from the guest bathroom. He told me twice.”
She puts her glass down on the rail. She takes the cuff of his sleeve — Theo’s sleeve — between her finger and thumb, and keeps it.
“Jack,” she says. “What’s up?”

choices.text: “It’s a pro-choice fundraiser, Skye. I can’t stand in it.”
choices.key: At the fundraiser Skye saw your face and asked twice. You told her straight out: you can’t stand in that room.
response: He says it to her, not to the view.

Behind them, through the glass, Gil is coming down off the stairs, and the banner hangs over him, and the trays go round with their cream cards. Skye turns and looks back through the window at all of it, and he can see her read it for the first time — the name, the cards, the glasses that went up.
“Oh,” she says. “Oh, *Jack*.”
“I’m sorry. It’s your night. I’m not sorry for the —” Her arm goes through his before he’s finished.

choices.text: “Five days ago I walked for the other side of this. You walked with me.”
choices.key: At the fundraiser Skye saw your face and asked twice. You told her five days ago you walked for the other side of this — and she walked with you.
response: She doesn’t say anything. She looks at him in the light from the house, and past him at the room, the banner, the glasses, and back at him.
Then she takes his arm the way she took it on the Embarcadero, high up, with both hands, and leans her weight into it.

choices.text: “I’m the only guy here who’d vote for the shrimp.”
choices.key: At the fundraiser Skye saw your face and asked twice. You made a joke about the shrimp — and then told her the truth anyway.
response: She laughs, out over the hills, and keeps hold of his sleeve, and raises her eyebrows at him: *and?*
So he gives her the real sentence anyway. “It’s a pro-choice fundraiser. I can’t stand in it.”
She’s still laughing a little when she takes his arm, both hands, up by the elbow, and turns him toward the door.

s04a.slug: THURSDAY · 7:36 PM · THE PALISADES — THE FRONT HALL
body: She doesn’t make a scene of it. It takes six minutes, and every one of them is gracious.

She walks him back through the room on her arm, not fast, smiling, a girl leaving a party early because she has somewhere better to be. At the foot of the stairs she stops for the host. “Gil,” she says, and takes both his hands, “thank you. The house is a dream.” She kisses Janine on the cheek. “You’ve got the best bartender in the Palisades,” she tells her. “Give him a show.” Janine laughs and says she’ll tell her husband, and looks at Jack, and at the arm, and says it was lovely to meet him. Jack says it was lovely to meet her too.
Corinne is where she was, at the near end of the bar, with a legal pad out now beside the BlackBerry and her pen going. Skye looks at her as they pass. Corinne looks back. The pen stops on the pad.

Outside, the motor court is lit up white. The photographer is gone; he got what he came for at five past seven. The valet is a kid from Santa Monica College in a red vest with a chemistry textbook open on the podium, and Skye folds a bill small and puts it in his hand and asks him, please, when the party closes, to bring the Saab down to the corner of Sunset and PCH and leave it under the heat lamp at the taco place.
The kid looks at her, and at the dark road going down the hill. “That’s, like, three miles.”
“We’re walking,” Skye says.

She steps out of her heels on the bottom step and hooks them on two fingers, and stands on the cold stone of the drive in her bare feet in the green dress, and looks up at Jack. Below the last of the roofs, past the black of the canyon, the lights of Sunset go down the hill in long loose curves to a place where they stop.
“Here’s the condition,” she says, and points a shoe at him. “You explain your politics the whole way down. All of it. Then you listen to me tell you why you’re wrong.”
“How far down?”
“To the ocean.” She starts down the drive ahead of him. “It’s downhill. You’ll live.”

s05.slug: THURSDAY · 7:45 PM · SUNSET BOULEVARD, THE PALISADES — DOWNHILL

body.text: “You can’t stand in it,” she says, swinging her shoes. “Okay. Tell me why while we walk. All of it.”
“The other side,” she says, swinging her shoes. “Okay. I walked yours. Walk me through it.”
“The shrimp has my vote too,” she says, swinging her shoes. “Now the real one. All of it.”

body: The hill road comes down out of the hedges in long switchbacks with no sidewalk, a white line and a gutter full of eucalyptus bark, and lets them out onto Sunset above the Village. The air has gone dry. Somebody up the canyon is burning oak, and the smoke comes down to the road thin and sweet, and the moon, most of the way to full, is well up over the hills behind them and follows them down.

At the first curve he takes off Theo’s jacket and holds it open behind her, and she backs into it without breaking stride and walks on with the sleeves down past her fingers and her heels hanging out of one cuff by their straps. Cars come up the hill at them with their brights on and dip them, one after another, out of courtesy or alarm.
So he tells her. It helps that it’s downhill.

“It’s a human being from the start,” he says. “That isn’t the catechism, that’s biology. Its own DNA the first day. A heartbeat by six weeks. Kevin has it in a textbook with pictures; he’ll show you, he’s dying to. That’s what we walked for in San Francisco — that, and nothing else. And I grew up in a union house. The Democrats came to the hall at election time and the hall went to Mass on Sunday, and every man in it would’ve walked out of that room tonight, and not because they’re Republicans. Pop would sooner eat his jacket. Because the life part used to be theirs too. Stupak’s what’s left of it. A Catholic Democrat from the Upper Peninsula who looked at his own party’s bill and said *not with that in it*, and held, and they had to come to him.”
She listens for most of a block, walking the top of the curb with her arms out and the empty sleeves hanging. When he’s done she hops down.

“My first show,” she says, “I was twelve, and I was somebody’s little sister. I had a catchphrase. I’m not doing it. The girl who stood in for my TV sister got bumped up to lines — nineteen, from Bakersfield, a morals clause in her contract and a mother who cashed her checks. She told me in the hair trailer, because I was a kid and I didn’t count. She didn’t say *pregnant*. She said, ‘I’m stuck.’” Skye walks on. “So who was going to pay for it? Stupak? The network had a lawyer, and her mother had the money, and the boy had a new phone number. That was the room, Jack. You couldn’t stand in Gil’s for an hour. She had to stand in hers.”
He opens his mouth.

“And don’t make that face. I’m not about to tell you that you hate women.” She points a sleeve at him. “You’d carry every woman in Los Angeles down this hill if she asked you nicely. You keep saying *the child*. I knew the girl.”
A car comes up out of the curve below, and its lights go over both of them, and she stands in them and waits for his answer.

choices.text: “She matters. So does the one she’s carrying. You don’t get to pick which one counts.”
response: “Neither does the network’s lawyer,” he says. “Neither does her mother.”

“See — you said *carrying*.” She turns around on the sidewalk and walks backward downhill in his jacket, facing him. “She said *stuck*. You’re arguing with a word she never used.” She tallies it in the air with a heel. “Mine.”
He goes looking for something to put against *stuck*, and comes back with nothing, and she watches him come back with it and turns around again, swinging the shoes.

choices.text: “Stupak’s a Democrat from the Upper Peninsula. It’s your party that can’t count to sixty.”
response: She stops walking. The jacket slides half off one shoulder, and she hitches it back up by the collar.
“That’s very good,” she says. “I’m stealing it for a dinner party. And she was still stuck, Youngstown. Sixty senators weren’t going to babysit.”
She bumps him off the curb with her hip and takes it back for herself.

choices.text: “You knew her. I didn’t. Tell me about her.”
response: So she does, walking. The girl kept it. The show didn’t keep her; they wrote her out in two lines and a suitcase, and she went home to Bakersfield. Skye was twelve. She sent a card with a stuffed giraffe taped to it, and never saw her again.

A driveway gate goes by. “If she’d asked me to drive her,” Skye says, “I’d have driven her. And cried the entire way. I don’t know why I’d have cried.” She moves the shoes to her other hand. “I never told anybody that part.”
He doesn’t argue with it. He moves to the traffic side of her, and keeps his hand at the small of her back down the next curve, where the sidewalk gives out.

choices.text: “Then argue the girl with me. What would it take for her to keep it? Who pays for that?”
response: Skye looks over at him from inside Theo’s collar. “Now you sound like a Democrat.”
“I sound like my mother’s parish. St. Brigid’s has a closet in the basement full of cribs and car seats, and a list of people who’ll drive you to the doctor, and Ma has the key to the closet.”

“Don’t,” Skye says. “Don’t be good at this. I had a speech about Republicans. It had a part in it for Glenn.” She pulls the lapels shut under her chin and walks on beside him, close enough to bump, and doesn’t give the speech.

s05a.slug: THURSDAY · 8:30 PM · SUNSET BOULEVARD, PALISADES VILLAGE — A BUS BENCH
body: Palisades Village has shut for the night: a bookstore with one lamp left on for a cat asleep in the window, a hardware store with its rakes chained out front, a café with the chairs upside down on the tables. Over the bank on the corner a clock trades the time for the temperature and back, and the temperature is fifty-one. Skye drops onto the bus bench under it — a realtor in a sport coat smiling across the backrest, BUYING OR SELLING? CALL MARTY — and swings her feet up into Jack’s lap as he sits down.
They’re like ice. He takes them in his hands and holds them, Theo’s cuffs riding up his wrists on their safety pins.
“Health care,” she says. “Go. Tell me you’re against it.”

“I’m for most of it. The insurance company can’t drop you for getting sick, or turn you down for what you’ve already got.” He rubs her arch with his thumb, and she shuts her eyes. “I’m against the abortion money. And I’m against it coming out of Washington, because nothing comes out of Washington without a string on it, and the other end of the string’s in somebody’s hand who’s never been to Ohio.”

“Massachusetts,” she says, eyes still shut. “Sixty is gone. The man with the truck took it.” She means the senator-elect’s pickup. It has been on every channel since. “So they pass the Senate’s, or they go home and explain it to people. I’m for it. All of it, the strings too. Strings are how you hold something up.”
“Strings are how you work a puppet.”
She opens one eye at him. She wiggles her toes in his hands.
“Your father’s union got him a doctor,” she says. “Whose union got Rudy one?”

It lands. Rudy at the flat-top at the Anchor in his hairnet, turning hash browns — Jack has worked that counter beside him since the fall and couldn’t tell you the name of his doctor, or if there is one. He sits on the bench under Marty with her feet in his hands and has no union to name.

choices.text: “Then pass it without the abortion money. Stupak’s language. Nelson’s isn’t the same thing.”
response: “Everybody in that house tonight knows Nelson’s isn’t the same thing,” he says. “That’s why they like it.”
“Sixty is gone, Youngstown.” She sits up and takes her feet back. “You get the Senate’s bill or you get nothing, and nothing doesn’t cover anybody’s teeth.”

He has an answer — the House can fix it, the House can wait — and she has one for his, about who’s waiting, and they go around it twice more under the bank clock while the temperature drops to fifty. It’s a draw. She won’t call it and he won’t either. She stands up, and holds a hand down to him, and pulls.

choices.text: “Rudy has a doctor. Her name is Gloria, and she prescribes pie.”
response: Skye folds in half on the bench, his jacket and all, her feet kicking in his hands, and a man walking two greyhounds on the far sidewalk stops and turns around to look.

When she can talk she sits up and wipes her eyes on a sleeve. “Rudy’s tooth, Jack.” She taps her own jaw, low on the left. “The night Gloria gave me the boysenberry. He chewed on the other side all night, and every time the door let the cold in he winced. I watched him.”
He reaches back for that night and can’t find the tooth anywhere in it. He holds on to her feet.

choices.text: “None did. You’re right.”
response: He tells her the true thing, the one he doesn’t tell people. Since Lordstown, the Costigans are on Ma’s insurance — the diocese’s plan, school secretary and dependents — and Pop, twenty-six years on the line, carries the card behind his union card in his wallet, where he doesn’t have to look at it. Pop hates it.
Skye takes her feet out of his lap and slides down the bench until she’s against his side, and puts her head on his shoulder.
“What does he say about it?”
“Nothing,” Jack says. “That’s what he says.”

choices.text: “I don’t trust Washington with my father’s pension. Why would I trust it with Rudy’s doctor?”
response: “Because the alternative is trusting Glenn Sato,” she says. “Or the guy Glenn buys his insurance from. I’ve met him. He has a boat in Marina del Rey called the *Deductible*. I’ve been on it. There was a cheese plate.”
It’s a real point, and it’s funny. He concedes the laugh and not the point, and says so, and she puts her cold feet back in his lap to show him what she thinks of that.

s05b.slug: THURSDAY · 9:15 PM · SUNSET BOULEVARD, TEMESCAL CANYON — THE LIGHT
body: At Temescal Canyon Road the light is red for a street with nothing on it. Up to the right the canyon goes back into the dark between its sycamores, the trunks white where the streetlight reaches them, and the air coming down out of it is colder by a coat and smells of wet sage. Skye presses the walk button three times.
“The bailout,” she says. “Let’s do one you’re wrong about.”
“I’m for it.”
She turns around from the button. “You’re *for* it.”

“GM goes under, Lordstown goes with it, and every bar and diner and parish for twenty miles goes with Lordstown. So yeah. I’m for it.” He hears Pop in it, and keeps going. “It didn’t save my dad. They took his shift in June, in the bankruptcy. It saved the plant. They still build the Cobalt out there. Good little car. There isn’t one in this zip code.” A Metro bus goes by them downhill, lit up inside and empty, NOT IN SERVICE across its forehead. “I’ll take the plant.”

“Okay. So.” She holds up one sleeve, a finger in it somewhere. “The men who run GM fly to Washington in their own jets to ask for money, and they get a bridge loan by Christmas. And the year before, the writers go out for three months, and every show in this town goes dark, and nobody bridges anybody anything. Not the writers. Not the crews. Not the woman who does craft services.” Another finger. “I’m a union member, Jack. Two of them. SAG and AFTRA. I paid dues before I could drive. Explain to me why the suits get a bridge and the people who build the thing get a pink slip and a speech.”
The walk sign comes on, white, and starts counting down, and she stands in front of it with Theo’s sleeve held up like a vote while it counts.

choices.text: “Because half the Valley eats off Lordstown, and nobody eats off a sitcom.”
response: “Tell that to the juicers,” she says.
“The what?”

“Juicers. Electricians. The guys up on the catwalks who hang every light you’ve ever seen me in.” The sign has run out under them, and she crosses anyway, against the red, with nothing coming. “They eat off a sitcom. They’ve got a union too, the IA, and when the writers went out they went home for three months with no check, and nobody flew anywhere to get them a loan.”
She says *juicers* like a word from her own kitchen, a word she had before she could read. He gets to the far curb a step behind her, and it’s her point, and he tells her so.

choices.text: “Two unions. You’re more labor than my father, and he’s got the jacket.”
response: “He has a *jacket*?” She lights up. “Describe the jacket.”
He describes it: LOCAL 1112 across the back, and the hook by the back door it’s hung on since June.

Skye turns Theo’s collar up, hunches down into it, sets her jaw, and turns into a man from Youngstown standing on a corner in Pacific Palisades and disapproving of it. “*Light’s red,*” she growls. “*You wait for the light. This isn’t Pittsburgh.*”
It’s terrible. It’s nothing like him. It’s so much him that Jack laughs until he misses the light, and loses whatever he was going to say about unions, and doesn’t go back for it.

choices.text: “Then we agree. The workers. Not the suits, not the studios.”
response: “The guys on the line in Lordstown and the guys on your catwalks,” he says. “Same guys. Different hats.”
She stops at the light. It’s green now. She doesn’t take it.
“Damn it,” she says.
“What?”

“I set that up and you walked right in and took it.” She looks at him in the green light with Theo’s collar up around her ears. “Fine. Yours.” And she holds it out to him in both hands, nothing in them, like a present she had been planning to keep for herself.

choices.text: “Your mother negotiated your contracts. Who was your union then?”
response: She keeps walking. Three steps, out ahead of him, into the crosswalk with the sign still counting.
“Nobody,” she says.

In the middle of Sunset, in the white bars of the crosswalk, she bends and fixes the strap of one of the heels in her hand. It doesn’t need fixing; she isn’t wearing it. Under Theo’s jacket her shoulders have come up a little toward her ears.
“That was cheap,” he says.
“It was good.” She straightens. “That’s the problem with you.” She walks on, and says the rest with her back to him, at the far curb: “Don’t do it twice.”
He catches up. Her shoulders are still up. They come down a block later, slowly, on their own, and he walks beside her and watches them until they do.

s05c.slug: THURSDAY · 9:55 PM · SUNSET BOULEVARD, THE LAKE SHRINE WALL — THE LAST HILL
body: The last hill runs down beside a long white wall with red tile along the top and bougainvillea spilling over it, mostly leaves this time of year. Behind it, Skye says, there’s a lake with swans on it, and a windmill somebody turned into a chapel, and a little bit of Gandhi in a stone box. “I did a shoot in there for a magazine. They were very nice about it. We weren’t allowed to smile near the ashes.”
She walks the curb along the wall with one hand trailing on the stucco.

“You want to know about that house?” she says. “That house is my people. Gil cries at his own pilots, and then he cancels them on Friday. Every person in that room ticked a box on a card tonight for anything with *choice* on it, and drove home, and half of them don’t have the woman who cleans the house on the insurance.” She doesn’t say it like a joke. “And you were at the lunch. Somebody two floors up from publicity called Corinne to ask, very nicely, whether Cassidy’s pro-life now. They don’t care what I believe, Jack. I could believe in Zeus. They want to know which half of the audience I cost them. That’s what a conviction is in that building. It’s a demographic.”
He has watched her work a room all night. He didn’t know she was keeping its books.

“So here’s yours.” She stops up on the curb, her eyes level with his. “You think you’re on nobody’s side. That side’s very expensive, Youngstown. It’s the side of everybody who’s never had to pay for one.”
“I’ve paid for one.”

“I read your Chesterton.” She jumps down. “The ordinary man ought to be in charge of the really important things — getting married, and kids, and the laws. That’s democracy, he says. And you read that and think, *ordinary man, that’s me, a guy from Ohio*. Jack. You walked out of a room tonight because you could. That girl from Bakersfield couldn’t walk out of anything.”

choices.text: “Nobody’s side isn’t a side. It’s a place you stand.”
response: “Where?” She puts her back to the wall and spreads her arms along it. “Show me where.”

So he tells her. In the pew at St. Brigid’s between Pop and Nonna, where the Democrats in the front and the Republicans in the back say the same Creed and mostly mean it the same. On Market Street five days ago, in sneakers, with her beside him. At the hall with his father in June, the week of the layoff, when nobody from either party came.
She opens her mouth to take it away from him. She shuts it again, and takes his arm instead, and they go down the last of the wall like that.

choices.text: “Says the girl who just walked out on a senator.”
response: “I walked out on a *shrimp*.” She points downhill with a shoe. “The senator wasn’t there. The senator was in Washington, being on a side.”
“The shrimp was there.”
“The shrimp had no position.”
They split it somewhere near the end of the wall, both laughing, and neither one could tell you who split it.

choices.text: “You knew all that and went anyway. Because it’s your job. Because they’re your people.”
response: She stops against the wall, her shoulder blades on the stucco and the shoes hanging off one hand, and looks back up the hill they came down.
“They’re my people,” she says. “Every one of them cries at pilots.”
It comes out fond, and it comes out like a prayer for a hopeless case, and she doesn’t pick. He takes the shoes from her, and carries them the rest of the way.

choices.text: “Then neither of us has a side. We’ve got each other’s.”
response: She stares at him. “That is so corny I want to report you to somebody,” she says. “I’ve been hit on by a man in a Pikachu suit on this exact boulevard, and he had better material.”
She takes his hand anyway, and laces her fingers through his, and swings it the rest of the way down the wall.

s05d.slug: THURSDAY · 10:40 PM · PACIFIC COAST HIGHWAY — WILL ROGERS STATE BEACH, THE LIFEGUARD TOWER
body: Sunset runs out at the bottom of the hill into the Pacific Coast Highway, four lanes and a median with the ocean on the far side of it, loud now, close enough to feel in the soles of his shoes. On the near corner the old gas-station kiosk sits under its heat lamp, the stools out front, the menu lit in the window, onions going on a flat-top somewhere inside it; the smell comes across the corner after them, and Skye turns her head to it and says, “Later,” like a promise to a dog. They cross with the light and go down a set of concrete steps past the empty lot, and the sand is cold and gives under them. A lifeguard tower stands up out of the dark on its legs, blue and white, shuttered for the winter, its ramp running down to the sand and the paint coming off the rail in flakes.

Behind them one car slows on PCH, a pair of headlights that drops below the speed of everything else and hangs there. Skye turns her face into his shoulder, quick, and keeps it there. The car picks up and goes on toward Malibu.

body.text: “Fine,” she says at the foot of the ramp, out of breath from nothing. “You win the hill. I win everything else on Sunset.” She counts it off on her fingers, his hand in her other one. “Rudy’s mine. The network’s mine. And you get the hill, because you argued it like you were carrying something up it instead of walking down.”

“You gave me two,” she says at the foot of the ramp. “On purpose. I’m going to be thinking about that all week.” She kicks sand at the bottom board of the ramp, and keeps hold of his hand through the whole kick.

“Draw,” she says at the foot of the ramp. “Pending a recount.” She holds out her hand, formally, and he shakes it, formally, on the sand, with the surf going off behind her like applause, and she keeps the hand afterward, which wasn’t in the terms.

body: She’s put the shoes down. They lie on their sides in the sand by the ramp, and Theo’s jacket hangs off her to the knees, and the surf breaks white behind her and runs up the beach and sinks into it.

“Everybody I know walks out of rooms,” she says. “I do it twice a week. I’m good at it; I’ve got a face for it. They walk out *away* from something.” She looks up at him. “You’re the only person I’ve ever seen walk out of a room *for* something.”

choices.text: *Kiss her.*
choices.key: At the bottom of Sunset, by a lifeguard tower, Skye said you’re the only person she knows who walked out of a room for something. You kissed her.
response: He doesn’t say anything to that. He kisses her, and walks her back with it until the rail of the ramp is behind her.

She makes a sound against his mouth, half a laugh, and her hands come up inside his collar, cold, and the jacket slides off her shoulders into the sand and nobody goes after it. His hands are on the rail on either side of her, and the pipe is ice under his palms, and he wants her hips in them instead, and the green dress gone, and the dark under the tower, and all night — he wants more than kissing, and he wants it all through him.
Up on the highway a truck goes by and leans on its horn at them, two long notes. Skye, without stopping, takes one hand off the back of his neck and waves.

choices.text: “I’d do it again. Every room.”
choices.key: At the bottom of Sunset Skye said you’re the only person she knows who walked out of a room for something. You told her you’d do it again, every room.
response: She has Theo’s tie in her hand before he’s done saying it, and walks him backward by it until the rail of the ramp is across his back, and kisses him.

The cold of the rail comes through Theo’s shirt in a stripe across his shoulder blades. Her hips are against his, and he puts his hands on them, on the thin green knit and the warm of her under it, and he wants — the dress up, and the jacket down in the sand, and her, here, under the tower, now — and the wanting goes through him from his mouth to his knees, and he lets it.
When she lets go of the tie it’s wrecked. She looks at it in the dark and puts her forehead against his chin.
“Ted’s going to kill you,” she says. “That was a *commitment*.”

choices.text: “Technically I walked out on a shrimp.”
choices.key: At the bottom of Sunset Skye said you’re the only person she knows who walked out of a room for something. You said technically it was a shrimp, and she kissed you anyway.

response.text: “I did that one already,” she says. “Up by Gandhi. It was better when I did it.”
response.else: “Technically,” she says, “the shrimp had it coming.”

response: She kisses him before she’s done laughing, so the start of it is mostly teeth. She pulls him in by his belt against her, against the rail at her back, and his hands go to her hips and find the green knit warm from Theo’s jacket and her under it, and he wants more than this — wants the dress up and the long dark under the tower and the rest of the night to spend in it.
A wave comes farther up the sand than the others and gets them both to the ankles, Theo’s trouser cuffs and all. Skye shrieks into his collar and doesn’t let go.

s06.slug: THURSDAY · 11:20 PM · TACOS EL FARO, SUNSET AT PCH
body: The radio sits on a shelf over the flat-top, a paint-flecked Panasonic with a coat hanger for an antenna, playing something old and slow with strings in it, and the cook sings the chorus under her breath while she scrapes down the griddle. Every time she throws meat on, the flat-top goes up in a hiss and a cloud, and the cloud comes out the window and hangs under the heat lamp with them.

Out on the old pump island there are two plastic tables now and four chairs that don’t match — two white, one green, one child-sized and red — and he and Skye have the lamp’s little orange room to themselves. Across the highway the surf is loud in the dark. Every few minutes a pair of headlights comes down Sunset, stops at the light, and turns north.

The cook’s name is Ofelia. It’s stitched over the pocket of her apron in red thread, under a red lighthouse to match the sign. When the two of them came across PCH out of the dark — Skye in the green dress with her heels hooked on her fingers, Jack in a borrowed suit with sand to the ankles — Ofelia leaned out of her window and said, “Ay, *mija*. Where are your shoes,” and then, “Sit. Sit, sit,” and fed them.

Skye ordered for both of them in a Spanish she says she learned from grips — mostly meat and swearing — and asked for extra limes. Ofelia rang up fifty cents for the limes and held her hand out for it, and Skye paid in quarters, one at a time, onto the little steel counter in the window.

“She charged me for limes,” she said when she sat down, looking at her two quarters’ worth on the paper plate like they’d come out of a mine. “Do you know how long it’s been since anybody charged me for a lime?”

Since then there’s been a second round, and a third for him, and his Mexican Coke in the glass bottle, and her horchata with the ice gone to slush, and the talk has gone everywhere the walk didn’t. Whether a hot dog is a taco: yes, she says, structurally; it’s a sandwich that won’t admit what it is, he says. Motels: her Barstow against his Erie, and Erie loses on the strength of a man who lived in the ice-machine alcove, until she does the Barstow night clerk for him, a man who answered every question with *That’s a policy*, and Barstow loses after all.

Somewhere in the second round Ofelia came out of the kiosk with a paper boat of grilled onions and one charred jalapeño they didn’t order, and set it in front of Jack. “*Para el flaco*,” she said, and went back in. He has been called worse. He ate the jalapeño to be polite and has been crying on and off ever since.
“What’s he singing about?” Jack says, about the radio.
“A man asking a woman to come back,” Skye says, listening with her head on one side. “It’s always that. Every language. They never write the one where she comes back and it’s fine.”

body.text: “You asked who my union was,” she says, with a lime in her fingers. “Here’s the other half.”
Out of nowhere, with a lime in her fingers, she says, “The juicers. At Temescal. I didn’t tell you why I knew the word.”
Out of nowhere, with a lime in her fingers, she says, “You know who hangs the lights? On a set? The guys up the ladders?”

“My father was a juicer. Pat Doyle. Meridian, mostly. Whatever stage was shooting, he was up over it on a ladder or out on the catwalk with a lamp the size of a trash can, and I was underneath in a car seat, I’m told. I don’t remember any of it.” She squeezes the lime over a taco that has had plenty of lime. “He left when I was four. Or he was made to. Depends which one of them you ask, and you can only ask one of them.”
body.else: “Juicers,” she says. “Electricians. The grips do the flags, and they’ll fight you if you mix them up — the juicers do the light. My father was a juicer. Pat Doyle. Meridian, mostly. Whatever stage was shooting, he was up over it on a ladder or out on the catwalk with a lamp the size of a trash can, and I was underneath in a car seat, I’m told. I don’t remember any of it.” She squeezes the lime over a taco that has had plenty of lime. “He left when I was four. Or he was made to. Depends which one of them you ask, and you can only ask one of them.”

body: “Your mother.”

“My mother took his name off everything. The mailbox. The bank. The hyphen.” She draws a short line in the air with the lime and rubs it out. “When I got my SAG card I was Skye Callender, and that was the first thing I ever signed. I was a kid. I practiced the *S* for a week.”
“What do you know about him?”

“He took his coffee with so much sugar the craft-service guy kept a separate jar for him, with *PAT* on it in tape. I got that from the craft-service guy.” She wipes her fingers on a napkin, one at a time. “He sent a card every birthday till I was nine, care of the studio. *Dad (Pat).* With the Pat in parentheses. Like I might need a footnote.”
“Did you ever see him again?”

“Once.” She puts the lime down. “I was fourteen. A pilot on Stage Nine — I was a girl who could hear dead people; it didn’t go. Between setups the gaffer leaned down to me and said, *Pat Doyle says hi*, and pointed up.” She points up, at the heat lamp. “There was a man on the catwalk with his hand up. Just up. Like a kid in class who knows the answer.” Her hand comes down to the table. “It’s a really big stage. Neither of us crossed it.”
“You wanted to,” Jack says.
“I was in a harness. For a stunt. I couldn’t have got up a ladder in it if I’d tried.” She laughs at herself, short. “That’s what I tell myself. The harness.”

Jack gets up and drags the green chair around the table, over the bolts where a pump used to stand, and sets it down against hers, and sits, so that their shoulders touch and they’re both facing the same way, out at the highway and the dark where the water is. She leans into him. For a while it’s the surf and the radio and Ofelia singing over the scraper.

Then she picks her phone up off the table, where it has been lying by the limes all night, and thumbs it awake, and scrolls up through today — *outside*, *theo says 5 more min*, *im timing him* — to Wednesday night, and turns it so he can see. There it is, the last thing before Thursday: *nonna wants your baptism name. if you have one.*
“You never answered it,” he says.

“I never answered it.” She looks at it on the little screen. “I’ve read it about forty times. In the car. In Gil’s guest bathroom, which has a view of Catalina, I’m told.” She sets the phone down by the limes. “I didn’t text it back because I wanted to say it out loud the first time.”
Over in the window Ofelia has stopped scraping to listen to the radio. A truck goes north on PCH and its wind comes across the pump island and moves the paper plates.
“Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle,” Skye says, in her own voice.
Jack doesn’t move. She keeps going, quickly.

“St. Mary’s, in Lancaster. I was six weeks old. There’s one picture, and I look furious about it. His mother was Mary Catherine — the grandmother. I met her twice. She called me all of it, both times, every syllable, like it was a title I’d won.” She tears the paper off her straw in a slow spiral. “My mother lost that one. She’s told me so. It’s the only thing I’ve got she didn’t name.”
She picks the lime back up.
“Ted knows,” she says. “Ted’s always known. He’s never used it.”

choices.text: *Say it back to her. All of it.*
choices.key: At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset, Skye told you her real name. You said it back to her, all of it.
response: He says it back to her across the plastic table, slowly, giving every part of it its own room, like Father Dom saying a name over the font at St. Brigid’s with the water already in his hand.
“Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle.”

She puts both hands over her mouth. Above them her eyes have gone wet. Then the grin comes up on him — he can feel it coming and can’t do a thing about it — and she takes her hands down and throws the lime at it. It gets him in Theo’s tie.
“*Mija*,” Ofelia says from the window, sorrowfully. “Those are fifty cents.”

choices.text: “Nonna’s going to love you. She’s going to love you *so much*, it’s going to be a problem.”
choices.key: At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset, Skye told you her real name. You told her Nonna’s going to love her so much it’s a problem.
response: “Good,” Skye says. “I want to be a problem for your grandmother.”
She rolls the lime under her palm on the tabletop, back and forth. “Will she?”
“She prays for Cassidy at the TV.”
“That’s not me.”
“She’ll fix it,” Jack says. “Give her a week. She’s been fixing people at that TV since Perry Mason.”

choices.text: “Mary Catherine. You’re named like a girl who wins the spelling bee.”
choices.key: At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset, Skye told you her real name. You said she’s named like a girl who wins the spelling bee — and then you said it properly.
response: “I’d have won it.”
“You’d have spelled *Callender* with one L to throw them.”
“I’d have spelled it with three.” She points the lime at him. “Go on. Do it right.”

So he does it right. He says it back to her across the plastic table, slowly, all of it — *Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle* — and she has to look away, at the radio, at Ofelia singing to it, before she can look at him again.

s06a.slug: FRIDAY · 1:10 AM · TACOS EL FARO — THE HEAT LAMP
body: The radio has gone to ads, a mattress store in Pico Rivera shouting about Presidents’ Day already, and Ofelia is wiping down the flat-top in long slow strokes, letting the grill go cold. “*Everything must go*,” Skye says, in the mattress man’s voice, right on his beat, and Ofelia says something to it in Spanish that the station would have to bleep. The Saab is at the curb under the lamp where the valet left it, top up, beaded with the wet coming in off the water.

A minute ago, before the ads, Skye asked him to send it. “Your nonna,” she said. “Tonight. Before I talk myself out of it.” He typed it on the RAZR with his thumb, and stopped after the second name, and she saw him stop. “The rest is yours,” he told her. “You give her that part.”
