body: “It’s after four there,” he says, the third time she asks him to check. “Gina’s asleep. Nonna’s asleep. The furnace is asleep.”
“Check again.”
He checks again. Nothing.
“What’s she going to do with it?” Skye says. “Your nonna. When she gets it.”
“Pray it.”
“Just like that.”
“That’s what she does with everything. Rain. Pop’s back. Me.” He shuts the phone. “She’s been praying for you since Christmas. Now she’s got the right name to do it under.”
Skye takes the RAZR out of his hand and opens it and checks it herself.
In the window Ofelia reaches up and switches off her sign, the red lighthouse and the word over it, and leaves the heat lamp burning for them.
“Corinne wanted a picture of us walking in,” Skye says. “She got one. A man in a fleece vest.” She gives him back his phone and picks up her own. “Come here.”

She takes him by Theo’s tie and stands him up and walks him to the window counter, and sits them on the two stools there, with the highway at their backs and the heat lamp up on its pole behind their heads. She holds the white iPhone out over the counter at the end of her arm, turned around on them, the little lens looking back, and she can’t see the screen and doesn’t try, and she doesn’t stop talking either. She is in the middle of explaining why Ofelia charging for limes is a moral position.
“It’s *respect*, Youngstown. It says, this lime has value, and so do you, and you are not special, and here’s your —”
He isn’t looking at the phone. He’s looking at her, at the lamp coming orange through the loose hair over her ear. The phone makes its little shutter sound.

She brings it in close to her face and tips it to the light and looks at it, and keeps looking, and doesn’t turn it around. When he reaches for it she holds it against her collarbone with her palm over the screen. When she finally looks up from it, it’s at him.
“Can I post this one instead?” she says. “The other one says you’re for something you’re not.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer. She saw my face from across the room and asked twice, and walked me out past the host and down Sunset to the ocean, making me explain myself the whole way and telling me why I’m wrong. She’s a union member. Two of them. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she told me about her father: Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name out loud. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. She asked before she posted us.

s07.slug: FRIDAY · 3:10 AM · US-101 NORTH, THE RINCON — THE SAAB
body: He wakes because the road has started to bend, and the sea is right there. The Rincon: the 101 running north along the edge of the continent, a guardrail and a scatter of riprap and then the Pacific, black, with the surf coming in white in long lines under a moon a night short of full. The top is up. The heater is on low. The iPod is off, and the radio is off, and there is nothing in the Saab but the tires and the water.

Skye is driving with her feet bare on the pedals and Theo’s suit jacket over her like a blanket, the sleeves hanging down either side of the seat. Somewhere since Malibu she has put her hair up with the rubber band off Ofelia’s to-go bag.
“You snore in Spanish now,” she says.
He sits up and scrubs his face with both hands. Up ahead the lights of Carpinteria are coming, a gas station lit white as an operating room, a sign for a motel with the *O* out.
“What’s your family going to say?” she says. “About the picture.”
She asks it easily, eyes on the road, but with her free hand she has pulled the jacket up to her chin.
He tells her the truth, because it’s the middle of the night on the Rincon and there isn’t anything else he’d want to tell her.

“Gina’s going to scream,” he says, “and then text me about it till chemistry. Ma’s going to say you’re beautiful. Pop’s going to grunt, which means you’re beautiful. Nonna’s going to say you’re beautiful and too thin, and ask what you eat, and not believe the answer.” The road bends, and the Saab leans into it, and comes out of it. “And then every one of them is going to ask me if you’re Catholic.”
He looks over at her, at her jaw in the green of the dash lights.
“Now I can say yes.”
Her right hand comes off the wheel and finds his knee in the dark, and grips it, and goes back to the wheel.

At the Delgado curb the building is dark except for the east stairwell, always lit, and the Saab idles. She kisses him across the gearshift, and again, and he gets a hand in her hair and the rubber band goes somewhere neither of them will ever find it, and she bites his lower lip, not hard, and kisses it better. Only kisses, slow ones, the windows fogging over around them.
At four she puts her hand on his chest, open, and pushes him back into his own seat.
“You have class.”
“It’s Friday.”

“You have *Friday*.” She shrugs Theo’s jacket off her shoulders and hands it across to him. “Tell Ted it had a nice time.” She reaches over him and opens his door herself. “Go be smart. I’ll call you when I wake up, which will be noon, because I’m famous, unless Corinne gets to me first.”
He gets out, and the cold finds him through Theo’s shirt, and he goes up the Delgado steps with the jacket over his arm. Halfway up he turns around to go back down to the car.
The curb is empty.
He stands on the step a long time, wanting to have gone back.

Theo comes in from the lobby with the iPhone held out ahead of him. “You’re a *photograph*, Costigan,” he says. “Again.” He has left the voice upstairs. He puts the phone in Jack’s hand with the page already up.

On the third floor, Theo, who was in the mailroom a few minutes ago, is sitting on the top step with his shoes against the wall, and Laney, who was at the far end of it, is leaning on the rail in the quilted vest with the pink BlackBerry held to her sternum like a hymnal. Neither one is looking at the other. Both of them are breathing very evenly.
“People remember the conversation they were *having*, Theodore,” Laney says, pitched for the back row of a ballroom, “not the one the other person was.”
“A fascinating point,” Theo says to the ceiling. “About memory. In general.”
“In *general*,” says Laney. “I read it in a magazine, Theodore.”
“Which magazine?”
“*Memory.* It was a whole issue.”

Jack could give them Book Ten of the *Confessions* from here, the fields and spacious palaces of memory, and they would let him. It sounds to him like a position paper on Wednesday, and he has no position. “Morning,” he says, and goes up past them.

On the fourth-floor landing he sits on the top step with his bag between his feet and opens the RAZR to his wall. On a RAZR a wall comes in stripes, four lines at a time, like a blind going up, and when it has finished the same two questions are at the top of it. Mrs. Pallante has asked hers. Tommy Hritz has asked his. Whichever one Jack answers, Glenwood Avenue will have it by lunch.
