s09.slug: FRIDAY · 1:15 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE BACK STEPS
body: The back steps of Hollis face the loading dock and the afternoon sun, and a dumpster that somebody in Art has painted with a dolphin, so they are warm by one o’clock and hardly anyone uses them. Jack takes the second one down with a Commons banana and his bag between his feet, forty minutes before his two o’clock.
The RAZR goes against his thigh before he has the banana open. GINA, across the little outside screen.
“Okay,” Gina says. “I have the late bus in eight minutes and I’m doing it in order.”
Behind her a row of diesels idles in the Ursuline lot with the heaters on, and a salt truck scrapes by, and a trunk slams.
“Hi, Gina.”
“Hi. Number one. Nonna. She said it nine times at breakfast. I counted under the table on my fingers. Rosie says ten, but Rosie counts the one she said to the toast.”
“It’s Mary Catherine,” Jack says.

“Not on Glenwood it isn’t. She made it Italian without being asked. She held the phone out at arm’s length like she was at the eye doctor and read it off the screen and kept going. Good crying. There’s two kinds, I’m an expert. Then she wouldn’t touch her eggs till somebody drove her to church, so we all went, before the 8:00 school Mass, and she went up the side aisle to Our Lady and put her money in and lit a tall one. Ma said *Mamma, we’ll be late*, and Nonna said *La Madonna non è mai in ritardo*, which means —”
“The Madonna’s never late.”

“I got a tardy slip for it. It says *family devotion*. And she looked up which Catherine in her missal, and it’s Alexandria. The wheel one. She out-argued fifty professors and they tried to kill her on a wheel. Nonna says Rome took her off the calendar in nineteen sixty-nine and put her back in two thousand two and never said sorry.”
“Fifty,” Jack says. “Did she win all fifty?”
“Nonna said *brava*. Out loud. To a saint.”

He thinks of Skye at a red light on Thursday with Nonna’s prayer going under her breath, and of Nonna in the side aisle at St. Brigid’s with her money in her fist: two women who have never met, working the same Madonna from either end of the country. The banana is half peeled, and he has forgotten it.

“Number two. Ma. She went down to the Dell in her coat before work and looked at the picture for a full minute. I was on the stairs. It wasn’t the Tuesday face, I know the Tuesday face. She said something about her size. I’m not repeating it, she’ll say it to you herself, it’s hers.”

body.text: “And Ryan Pallante texted me. Ryan has not texted me since the fifth grade. *My mother printed your brother’s yes and put it on the refrigerator under St. Joseph.* With the period in it, Jack. He’s mortified.”

body: “And everybody at school keeps asking is she Catholic, and does she pray, and is she nice in real life, and not one of them asked about —”
“Gina.”
He pulls the banana the rest of the way open.
“— the *weather*,” Gina says. “Out there. Jeez. I was going to say the weather.”
“Number three. Did you mail it?”
“This morning. The slot in the mailroom.”
“Then it’s late. It goes in with mine Monday, and then it sits in their mailroom while a CO reads your handwriting, so it’s *very* late. That’s fine. Late’s fine. Mine has a candle on it.”

“Number four. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday and I’m coming. Ma said yes if my chemistry’s done by Saturday night, so it will be. I’m telling him the name. In person, across the table. He’s going to *lose it*.”
“Wait till he’s eaten something.”
“Obviously after. I’m not an animal.”
Behind her the air brakes let go, and the doors fold open on their long hydraulic sigh, and a driver somewhere calls *Let’s go, ladies*.
“Bus. That’s mine — I love you, that was on a bus, it doesn’t count.”
The doors thump shut on her end, and the RAZR goes back to being a phone.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first. Monday she found me on a celebrity blog before I did, and knew Danny’s jacket. A man from Mahoning County called Danny a name in the comments; she reported him, answered him, and called him one back — a Catholic one. She’s making Danny a card for Candlemas. Tuesday Ashley Vrabel showed her the picture in chem. Capitals. Wednesday, at three in the morning her time: Nonna wants a baptism name, for the rosary. Friday she was lowercase again: *mary catherine?????* Nonna said it nine times at breakfast and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. My Candlemas card for Danny goes in her envelope Monday. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday. She’s telling him in person.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.* Thursday night I sent Gina the name: Mary Catherine. At breakfast Nonna said *Maria Caterina* nine times, and cried the good kind, and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 4:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — THE GAG
body: Doug is waiting at the top of the stairs in socks and a Horde T-shirt, and he says “Duuuuude” before Jack is off the last step, with every vowel he owns. Room 420 has a gap in it where Doug’s desk chair used to be, until Tuesday, when Doug stood on the chair to kill a moth. The fourth-floor lounge has a spare futon frame. The raid is at seven.
“You didn’t bring me one,” Doug says on the way down the hall. “The taco. I said on the internet.”
“It was midnight in the Palisades, Doug.”
“Dude. They have *foil*.”

The lounge has one tall window, and the sun is low enough now to come straight in through it and lay a bar of low sun across the carpet and up the wall where the futon frame leans, all slats and dowels. On the television bolted up in the corner, with the sound turned down to a murmur, the President is at a lectern in a hotel ballroom taking questions from rows of House Republicans, a replay from the morning; the banner under him says Baltimore. Yusuf is on the arm of the couch with a paperback. On the couch is Laney, with her laptop on her knees, and beside her Lena, in socks, with her feet up under her and a legal pad against her knees and a pen going. Greene’s *The End of the Affair* lies shut on the coffee table in front of her with a bookstore receipt sticking out of the back cover.
Jack didn’t check. It’s his floor; 217 has a floor of its own. He crosses to the far wall and gets his hands under his end of the frame.
“Yusuf won’t take the other end,” Doug says. “He says it’s a matter of conscience.”
“I said it’s a matter of my back.” Yusuf turns a page. “Also I’m in mourning.”
“For the *Catcher in the Rye* guy,” Doug tells Jack.

“People have been coming up to me since breakfast like I’m the next of kin.” Yusuf tips the paperback up so the cover shows: *Nine Stories*, an old drugstore copy with the spine broken in three places. “I never read *Catcher*. I read the good one.”
“Dude, *Catcher*’s the good one. It’s the one with the hat.”
“It’s the one everybody read,” Yusuf says. “That’s a different thing.”

Priya goes past the doorway with a laminate under her arm, stops, comes back one step and says into the room, “Per the Residential Life Handbook, lounge furniture is *lounge* furniture, Doug.” Doug holds up a pink carbon with her signature at the bottom of it. Priya reads it to the end, including the fine print. She wrote it. “The fifth,” she says. “Not the sixth, Doug.” She takes the laminate on down the hall toward 401.
They have the frame off the wall and are turning it end for end, slowly, to clear the television, when Laney stops scrolling.
“Oh,” Laney says. “Oh, no. Oh, *bless* her heart, no.”
She clicks, and the screen fills with a picture. Jack knows it from across the room by its colors.

Laney puts one hand to her throat. With the other she lifts the laptop off her knees and holds it out level at the end of her arm, like a tray she has been asked to carry out of a burning building, and then she dies. It is not quick. She goes over sideways across the far arm of the couch by stages, a dying swan in a Pi Lam sweatshirt: the back of her free wrist to her forehead, one leg rising, the toes pointed, the knee giving way, the laptop held up above her the entire time without a wobble, until she is hanging upside down off the arm with her hair on the carpet.

“I can’t,” she says. “I *can’t*. Tacos. She posted *tacos* at him.” Her head drops the rest of the way back. “Somebody call Tammy Price in Dallas and tell her her baby girl died of a taco. In California. Which she *warned* me about.”
And Lena laughs.

She has her mouth shut on it, hard, her lips pressed together, and it gets out anyway, through her nose: one short, loud, unlovely snort, the kind a person lets go of in the third pew at a funeral. Her eyes go wide at it. She is furious with her nose, and it’s all over her face, and behind the fury her mouth comes open anyway and the rest of it starts up out of her, real and helpless, her shoulders going —
— and her eyes come up over Laney’s hip and find the doorway, and find Jack in it with his end of the futon.

It goes out of her face from the top down. Her eyes first, then the color, then her cheeks; her mouth is the last part of her to get the news, still open on the shape of the laugh after the rest has gone, and then it closes too. She takes the cap off the coffee table and puts it on her pen and presses until it clicks. She picks up the Greene and sets it down again square to the edge of the table, and leaves her hand on the cover.
Jack has a futon to move.
“Lift on three,” Doug says. “Dude. *Three.*”

Laney is still hanging off the end of the couch, and she isn’t looking at the laptop anymore, or at Lena. She’s looking at Jack, down the length of the room: a long look, unreadable, her face going red from hanging upside down. Contempt, he figures; he’s had two weeks of it. He takes his end up on three.

They get it through the door on the second try. Doug walks backward with the light end, steering by his heels, and Jack has the heavy end and carries it down the corridor like it weighs what a broom weighs, past the trash chute and Priya’s bulletin board and the door of 412. At the turn Doug says, “Dude, *pivot*,” drawing it out to the length of a sentence, and Jack pivots, and the corner of the frame finds the doorjamb of 420 and takes out a chip of paint the size of a quarter.

Doug puts a fingertip on the bare wood. “That was there,” he says. “Dude. That was *there* before.” Inside, on his thirteen-inch, a tauren in plate armor stands by himself in the snow of Northrend, waiting for seven o’clock.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time.

s10a.slug: FRIDAY · 4:58 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL
body: The landing windows in the east stairwell open six inches and then meet a bolt, put in by Residential Life the year somebody tried for seven. Jack pushes the one between four and three up until it meets it. Down in the lot the sun has gone long and gold across the windshields, and out on the asphalt a kid on a skateboard keeps trying the same curb: the wheels clack off it, a pause, again.

It comes up in his mouth first, and then in his fingers. The pack is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt with the lighter, and his hand is in there with it, holding it through the lining. The tin rides in the other pocket, against his hip, with its corners. Out in the lot the skateboard comes off the curb and goes down hard, and the kid lies on his back on the warm asphalt and laughs at the sky.

choices.text: *Light one.*
choices.key: On the east stairs Friday afternoon, you lit one.
response: He lights it in the gap with his shoulder against the frame and blows the first pull out through it, and the wind coming across the lot takes the smoke sideways, over the bike racks and the dumpsters and away toward the beach. He smokes it down with his forearms on the sill and the cold coming in over his wrists. He doesn’t think about anything.
He puts it out on the outside ledge and pockets the end. Below him the kid is up again, and lands the curb, and rolls off down the row of cars with both arms in the air.

choices.text: *Put it back.*
response: He takes his hand out of the jacket with nothing in it. The pack goes back down into the lining. He leaves the window up and stands in the cold coming through the gap with both hands on the sill, until his fingers quit asking, and the kid in the lot gets up and tries the curb again, and falls again, and gets up.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them.*
response: He takes out the tin instead and opens it on the sill. RELIQUARY, on the lid, in marker. He counts them in the last of the sun with one fingertip.
Eleven.
He shuts it and puts it back against his hip.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 8:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The Fishbowl is the one room in Delgado with a glass wall, so that Residential Life can see in, and at half past eight on a Friday there is a great deal to see. On the television a woman with a gift for the afterlife is standing in a child’s bedroom telling a radiator *I know you’re still here*, and the room has its back to her. Priya’s table by the door has a new laminate up beside the guest ledger, ALL GUESTS SIGN IN. ALL., and in the ledger, in a round actress’s hand, under *Visiting* it says *412* and under *Purpose*, *ghost*. Priya studied it and let it stand.

Skye is on the arm of the middle couch in Jack’s flannel with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, telling Thursday to the room in parts. She does the host, whose every consonant is billed by the hour. She does the host’s wife, whose cheek she kissed at the foot of the stairs, and who, according to Skye, knew to the dollar what it cost. She does the walk down Sunset in bare feet, the realtor on the bus bench (BUYING OR SELLING?) and the bank clock that trades the time for the temperature, and Jack in Theo’s pinned trousers explaining Stupak to both of them. She does a shrimp on a spoon: its dignity, its rising dread. Doug lies on the carpet with a cushion under his head and says “On a *spoon*?” at the pauses. Theo, at the far end of the couch in the blue blazer, laughs on every beat and half a beat late. Jack was there. He wouldn’t have it any other way, since she tells it better than it went. She has had four hours of sleep and a morning of Corinne and she is the best thing in the room. Jack is aware this is not an objective assessment.
“I have a methodological concern,” says Margot, from the armchair, when the shrimp has been eaten.
“Put it next to the shrimp,” Skye says. “He’s been very good.”

“I’m in favor of the walk. In the abstract I’m in favor of any woman leaving any room.” Margot has her notebook on the arm of the chair. “My difficulty is structural. A woman leaves a fundraiser where the toast was to a woman’s right to choose, in an election year, because her boyfriend is uncomfortable with the subject. I’m not accusing you of bad faith. I’m accusing you of a *narrative*. Every person in that house had the story before you reached the valet, and it wasn’t *she’s loyal*. It was *she picked him*. And you can’t un-arrive. A man in a fleece vest got you at the door with your hand on his arm, and by nine it was on the internet. That picture says you came for the cause. The walk says you left it. You are going to have to live in both.”
“I didn’t walk out on Boxer,” Skye says. “I walked out with *him*.” She tips her head at Jack. “I’m still voting for her. He never asked me to go. I took his arm.”

“Which is precisely what a woman says, and precisely how it gets read. Voting is private. A body in a room is public, and a body leaving a room is a text, whether or not it meant to be one. You may intend the first with perfect sincerity and the second will still be read as a statement.” Theo’s eyes go to Jack and back to the ghost.

At *a body in a room* Kevin gets to his feet, says, “I need a pretzel,” and goes out through the glass door to the vending machine in the hall, where he stays, visible from every couch, selecting. He puts in a dollar, takes it back out, and puts it in again.
“The picture I put up instead was so I wouldn’t make *him* say something he doesn’t believe,” Skye says. “I don’t put words in people’s mouths. I get paid when other people do it to me.”
Margot looks at her for some time. “That is an ethics-of-attribution point,” she says, “and it’s a good one. I’ll give you the post. One point. I’m keeping the other one. It’s load-bearing.”
“Keep it,” Skye says. “I’ll come back for it.”
“I expect you will.” Margot slides the Fishbowl’s one clean mug across the coffee table to her. It has tea in it. Skye drinks it.
“The valet, I’m told, is torn,” Theo offers.
“Costigan.” Margot turns on him. “You have been very quiet for a man whose politics caused an incident.”
“I’m enjoying it,” Jack says. “And she’s right about the room. They did read it that way.”
“Traitor,” Skye says.
“I’m on your side. She’s still right about the room.”
“Keep going. I’m collecting.”
Margot ignores them both. “I would like it noted that the feminist outcome of the evening was a woman rescuing a man from a cocktail party, and that I can’t use it.”
“Write it up anyway.”
“Chivalry, Reversed. With a footnote about the shrimp.”
Doug raises one hand from the carpet. “Was there, like, a little quiche?”
“A spoon, Doug.”
“Right. Right. On a spoon.”

The argument runs through a commercial break and out the other side into a second ghost. Skye, with a hand on Jack’s neck and one bare foot found against his calf, leans in during the ads and says something into his ear in the host’s voice that he will be getting over until Tuesday. Then she watches the television for a while with her head on one side. “She has a *window* in that scene,” she says, “and she’s playing it to the radiator.”
“Dude, it’s a ghost,” Doug says.
“It’s still a window.”

At eleven by the clock over the sign-in table she slides off the couch arm and into her coat, and Priya already has the pen held out on its string. She signs herself out. Under *Purpose*, in the round hand: *achieved*. “Please come again,” Priya says, and then, frowning at herself, “That’s not on the laminate.” At the door she turns back to the room. “Saturday. Daylight. Bring the clipboard for Fenner,” she tells Jack, and kisses him, once, quick, in front of everybody, and Doug applauds alone.
“Thank you, Douglas.” She looks down the couch. “Ted.”
“Skye.”
“Sunday.”
“You told me. Twice,” Theo says, short, and it gets out the door before she does.

Through the glass Jack watches her cross the lobby, and Marcus at the front desk watch her all the way to the street door. In the hall Kevin has finally selected and is eating a pretzel, one at a time. When Jack turns around Theo has moved down the couch to him without seeming to move, and is watching the ghost.
“You walked her out,” Theo says, low.
“She walked me out.”
“That’s worse, Costigan.” Now he looks over. “That’s *love*.”

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the walkout. Skye said she didn’t walk out on Boxer, she walked out with me, and she’s still voting for her. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture.

choices.text: “Yeah. It is.”
choices.key: In the Fishbowl Theo said walking out with her was love. You said yes, it is.
response: Theo looks at him for a while, and then at the television, where a ghost is being helped toward the light. “Well,” he says. “Mazel tov.”

choices.text: “Put it on a plaque. Brass. Serif.”
choices.key: In the Fishbowl Theo said walking out with her was love. You told him to put it on a plaque.
response: “I’ll have it engraved,” Theo says. “WALKED OUT, EST. 2010. Margot will say brass is a choice.”
“Brass is a choice,” Margot says, from across the room, without looking up.

choices.text: “She’s the answer, Theo. I told you.”
choices.key: In the Fishbowl Theo said walking out with her was love. You told him again she’s the answer.
response: Theo doesn’t argue. He finds the remote in the cushions and turns the ghost up.

body: A clear Saturday, and the town has come out to stand in it. The sky over the Point is scrubbed hard and pale, the storms have left the kelp in black heaps along the tide line, and out past the rocks the swell comes in from the northwest in long clean lines, with the wind off the land combing the spray back off their tops. Down by the dark Light the low wall is already warm through Jack’s jeans.

Pair 41 has set up at the north end of it: Fenner’s form on the clipboard, one pencil, a stopwatch signed out of the department with PROPERTY OF MORRO 1100 scratched into its back with a key, and a paper bag from the bakery on Seacliff Road that held four Danish at ten o’clock and holds one now. The method is Fenner’s. Pick a rock. Time each crest as it crosses the rock, ten in a row, write them down, do it again from the next station along the wall. Skye has the pencil because she has the handwriting. She also has his flannel from the Walk on, over a gray sweatshirt that says SWEETWATER ACADEMY CREW. She took it from wardrobe in 2008 and calls it the only honest thing she owns.
Out in the lineup a dozen surfers sit their boards in the swell, black in their wetsuits, waiting. One of them goes for a wave too early, and it goes on without him.

“He’s going to go for this one, Jim,” Skye says, very low, in the hush of a golf announcer at the eighteenth green, a man in a blazer who has never once raised his voice at a wave. “A bold choice. A young man’s choice.” Below them the young man comes up out of the white and shakes his hair out of his eyes. “He’ll want that one back.”
Jack clicks the stopwatch. “Eleven.”

“The young man is eleven.” She writes it down. “And now, Jim, the veteran. Gray at the temples. Look at that patience. He has waited forty minutes for this, and he’ll go home and tell his wife about it, and she won’t listen.” The older man drops into a clean right and rides it nearly to the rocks, and Skye breathes, “Oh, that’s *lovely*,” and writes down *twelve*.

They do ten. They move down the wall to the second station, past the white cross at the end of it, where last Sunday’s roses are still tied to the fence wire, gone brown on their kitchen string. They do ten more.

body.text: “This is the daylight column,” she says, writing down a set. “I’m living in it. It’s very bright. I don’t know how you people stand it.”
body.else: “This is daylight,” she says, writing down a set. “I’m told it’s good for you.”

body: Fenner wants to know why the Point breaks where it does, and Jack has the answer off the lecture slides: the shoal under the Point, the end of each wave that feels the bottom first and slows down, and the rest of the line swinging around to catch up with it, so that every set coming in off the open water bends toward the Point and stands up here, in front of them.
“So it bends toward the slow part,” Skye says.
“That’s refraction.”
“That’s the most romantic thing Fenner has ever said, and he said it about sediment.” She puts the pencil behind her ear and takes the last piece of Danish without offering it.
He tells her about the candle while she’s eating it: Nonna lit one. A tall one, up the side aisle at St. Brigid’s before the school Mass, with the whole family late for it.
“A candle,” Skye says. “For me.”
“For Maria Caterina.”

He says it the way Nonna says it, every vowel open, the *r* turned over once on the tongue. Skye stops chewing. She looks out at the lineup, where nothing is happening, for long enough that the veteran paddles back out past the break.

“Maria Caterina,” she says, finally, reaching for a bit, “sounds like a woman who runs a bakery and has opinions about your —” and that’s as far as she gets with it. She shuts her mouth on the rest and shakes her head at herself, and wipes one eye with the cuff of his flannel, fast, like it was spray.
“Say it again,” she says. “The Italian way.”
He says it again. She says it after him under her breath, and gets the *r* wrong, and then right.
When the next set is written down she taps the pencil on the clipboard. “I’m sitting where I sat last week,” she says, to the form. “Tomorrow.”
“Same pew.”
“Same pew.” She nods, a scheduling matter, settled, and that’s all either of them says about tomorrow.

Out at the first rock the swell lifts again, three lines deep, and he clicks the stopwatch. The first one feels the shoal and slows, and the rest of it comes around to meet it, and it breaks where it does. “Nine,” he says, and she writes it down.

journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Skye, till May. No trades. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown. Tuesday: half of Pair 41. Wednesday: field data from the lot in a storm — it wasn’t breaking where it does. It was breaking everywhere. Sunday: the Point open again — breaking where it does. Saturday at the Point with Fenner’s form and a stopwatch, timing the sets. Skye called the surfers like the last hole of a golf tournament. Breaking where it does.

s13.slug: SATURDAY · 6:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE OTHER TIE
body: The sun is down, and 412 is blue except for the desk lamp, and under the window the curb has begun to fill with heels.

Theo has tied the navy silk four times in the full-length mirror and undone it four times, and on the fifth he gets as far as the second turn, stops, and takes it off over his head. The hands that can deal a deck, split a lime with a thumbnail and open a Rioja with a shoe will not do this one thing tonight. He holds the tie out without turning around. “Costigan.”

Jack gets up off his bed. He is in jeans and a Marisol sweatshirt, off a short shift at the Anchor at five with the flat-top still in his hair, and he has nowhere to be, a fact he keeps finding in his pockets like a twenty.
“Last offer,” Theo says. “Pi Lam has a surplus of girls with minors in Italian.”
“I’m good.”

Jack stands behind him, the two of them in the mirror, Thursday with the parts swapped, and does it: over, under, through, the half-Windsor, drawn up to a finger’s width of the collar. “It’s a commitment,” he says, working the knot.

“Don’t quote me to me.” Theo lifts his chin for the collar. “The theme tonight is *A Night in the Alps*, in a county where it is sixty-eight degrees. The Alps are two thousand dollars of foam. There is a machine that makes snow. It is soap, Costigan, and at ten o’clock a girl in a strapless dress will run out into it with her arms up and be, for forty seconds, entirely happy, and I would not take that from her for anything.” Downstairs his date is waiting at the front desk. He watches Jack’s hands in the glass, and out of nowhere: “Costigan. Do you know what you’re going to say tomorrow? If she asks.”
Jack’s hands finish the knot. “She’s going to ask.”
“That’s not what I asked.”
In the mirror, over Theo’s shoulder, Jack has nothing to put in his face. He sets the collar down over the knot and smooths it with both thumbs, and Theo lets him, and they both study the tie.

Then the voice comes back on like a porch light. “I shall be at the Pi Lam house being asked what my father does, by people who know,” Theo says. “Don’t wait up. Or do, Father Jack. It’s a free country, and you have a lamp.” He takes the blazer off the chair, and goes.

Jack goes to the window. The moon is coming up over the ridge behind Engineering, full and still orange from the ground, so big it looks nearer than the ridge, and he watches it climb the oaks. At the bottom of the glass, at the edge of what he is looking at, Brooks Callahan’s black Tahoe is idling at the curb with its hazards going, and Laney comes down the Delgado steps under the porch light in gold sequins and a wrap she has no intention of wearing. Lena, in a gray sweatshirt, comes after her with the wrap over one arm. At the curb she takes the last inch of the zipper in both hands and finishes it, and Laney lifts her hair off her neck in the pageant gesture to let her. Then the Tahoe door, and Brooks around it, and the gold goes in, and an arm comes out of the back window for the wrap, and Lena puts it there. When the car pulls away the sweatshirt goes back up the steps.
The moon is clear of the ridge. Ma’s red tie has waited since Thursday. Jack hangs it over the back of the desk chair, where he will see it at seven.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You walked her out.” She walked me out. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 10:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE BLUFF STAIRS, FULL MOON
body: Through the screen door of Sol’s house Tomás has something old going on the stereo, brushes on a snare and a steel guitar and a man singing high and thin, and it comes out across the porch and goes on past them down the bluff toward the water. The moon is up over the ocean, full, white as a plate, bright enough that Jack can read the Surfrider sticker on the porch rail. Sol’s swing is back on its hooks on the new chain, and Skye is in it with her knees pulled up inside a cream fisherman’s sweater that comes to the middle of her thighs, bare legs, bare feet, pushing herself off the boards with one toe.
“You’re late,” she says.
“It’s ten-fifty. You said ten-thirty.”
“I said ten-thirty and I meant ten. I wanted you early.”

He doesn’t have an excuse, so he gives her news instead: he tied Theo’s tie tonight. She stops the swing with her heel to hear it, and he gives her all of it: the foam Alps, the soap snow, the girl who will run out into it at ten o’clock with her arms up.

“Ted at a formal,” she says. “He’ll be the only man there with a pocket square and an exit plan. We went to a premiere together when we were twelve and he left during the speeches. Out a bathroom window. In a clip-on.”
“He gave me a speech about the snow.”
“That’s crying, for Ted.” She gets up off the swing. “Come see the stairs. Tomás fixed the bottom one. He wants it noticed.”

The bluff stairs go down the cliff behind the house in three crooked flights, gray boards gone soft with salt and a two-by-four for a rail, and at the bottom the beach lies pale under the moon all the way to the Point, and the surf comes in loud and white and slides back hissing. She goes first, barefoot, not holding the rail. Four steps down she stops and turns around on the step below him, so that her eyes come level with his, and kisses him.

It goes on a long time. The music comes down the bluff in pieces, whenever the wind allows it. He gets his hands up under the sweater and there is nothing under it but her: the small of her back warm under the wool and cold at the edges where the night has got in. He spreads his hands over her shoulder blades and brings her up the step into him, and she makes a sound against his mouth. Her own hands go inside his flannel and up under his T-shirt, and they are freezing, and he flinches, and she hums, pleased with herself, and keeps them there, spread over his ribs, until they warm.

His thumbs find the bottom edge of her ribs and follow it around, slowly, and her breath goes short against his cheek. She puts her mouth to his throat under the hinge of his jaw, teeth and then not teeth. The step is too narrow for two people. Her thigh is between his, and the rail is in his back, and when she leans her weight into him the flight of stairs creaks from top to bottom. He hears himself say her name into her hair.

They don’t make it down the rest of the way so much as arrive. At the bottom she pulls him onto the sand, and it is cold through his jeans and cold under his palms, and she comes down into his lap facing him with her knees in the sand on either side and the sweater riding up her thighs, and kisses him again, slower, both hands on his face. The moon is behind her on the water. He has his hands under the wool on the warm bare skin of her back, and every part of him knows where they would go next, and wants them there. There is her weight, and the cold, and the sound she makes when his thumbs go along her ribs again. She shifts in his lap, once, and they both feel where that would go, and she stops, and puts her forehead down on his and laughs, unsteadily, at both of them.
He pulls back far enough to see her. Her mouth is wet and her hair is full of wind and moon, and the next words are coming up in him before he has them, and he knows exactly what they are.
“Skye —”
She puts two fingers over his mouth.
“*Tomorrow*,” she says. Her breath isn’t steady. Her fingers are. “I gave my word. You don’t get to make me break it the night before.”

choices.text: *Say it anyway, against her fingers: “Tomorrow, then.”*
choices.key: Saturday night on the bluff you almost asked. Skye kept her word — tomorrow — and you said it back against her fingers.
response: “Tomorrow, then,” he says, against her fingers, so that she feels it more than hears it.

She takes the fingers away and kisses the place where they were. Then she gets up off him, and pulls him up by both hands, sand pouring out of his flannel, and at the foot of the stairs she holds his face in both hands while Tomás’s record comes down to them on the wind.

choices.text: *Kiss her fingers. Let her keep her word.*
choices.key: Saturday night on the bluff you almost asked. Skye kept her word, and you let her.
response: He kisses her fingers where they lie over his mouth, and that is his answer.
She takes them back and looks at them in the moonlight. “That isn’t fair either,” she says. She climbs off him and sits down on the bottom step in the sweater, and points up the stairs with her chin.
He goes up on his own. At the top, with the screen door letting the record out again, he looks down, and she’s sitting on the bottom step with her arms around her knees.

choices.text: *Ask anyway.*
choices.key: Saturday night on the bluff you asked anyway. Skye said no — laughing — for your sake.
response: He takes her hand away from his mouth by the wrist and keeps it, and asks. He doesn’t dress it up. “I don’t want to wait till tomorrow.”

“No,” she says, into his mouth, laughing, kissing him through it, “no, no, absolutely not, no —” and keeps on until he’s laughing too, his forehead against hers. “You’d be sorry by the Gospel,” she says, “and I’d have to sit there and watch you be sorry.”
She gets up, and hauls him up after her, and pushes him up the first three steps by the seat of his jeans.

s15.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE FOURTH SUNDAY
body: The 11:30 is the Mass for the late, the hungover and the young families, and the sun comes in through the high clear windows of St. Brendan’s in long slanting bars and lies across all three. Out in the courtyard somebody has taped a Catholic Schools Week banner to the parish-hall door in blue and gold, and it has already begun to curl. Jack is wearing Ma’s red tie. It has finally got its pew.

Skye is already in the one where she sat last week, halfway up on the Mary side, on the aisle so he can get out. She has on a gray cardigan buttoned to the throat over a white collar, and her hair pinned up, and no makeup he can find. When she leans forward to put the kneeler down a price tag rides up out of the back of it on its plastic thread — $68, and the name of a store on State Street — and he reaches over and tucks it back under the wool with one finger.
She keeps her eyes front. “I bought it for this,” she says. “Don’t look at it.”

Mrs. Fitch’s bulletin is in the hymnal rack, clip-art angels blowing trumpets around the Mass times, and while the procession comes up the aisle Skye takes it out and reads it to the end — the Knights’ pancake breakfast, the CYO car wash, the prayer list — and puts her finger on a name under PLEASE PRAY FOR, a stranger in Lompoc, and keeps it there through the opening hymn.
Jeremiah first, read by a man from the choir: *before I formed you in the womb I knew you*. Skye’s eyes come sideways to Jack, a week after San Francisco, and go back.
Bridget McNulty from Newman reads the second reading, in a navy skirt, holding the edges of the big book like a railing.
*“Love is patient, love is kind.”*

She goes on down the list of everything it isn’t — not jealous, not pompous, not rude — and Jack stops at the first word. *Patient.* He looks at Skye’s hands. They’re folded in her lap, right thumb over left, the fingers that were over his mouth twelve hours ago lying still on her knee. All week she has kept the word she gave him on Monday, and she has kept it better than he would have.

Father Osei reads the Gospel himself: Nazareth turning on its own boy. *Amen, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own native place.* They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill to throw him off it, *but he passed through the midst of them and went away.* Osei closes the book and stands at the ambo with no notes.

“They could not hear him in Nazareth because they already knew him,” he says. “The carpenter. Joseph’s boy. The one who borrowed a ladder and did not bring it back. It is very hard to be heard by people who are sure they know you — and notice that he does not argue with the hill. He passes through the midst of them, and he goes on.”
He sits down.
Skye leans over. “That’s it?” she whispers. “He’s done?”
“He doesn’t go long.”
“I’ve had longer notes from a grip.”

At the sign of peace the old man in the pew behind them shakes Skye’s hand like a deacon and says, “Peace be with you, young lady,” and she says, “And also with you,” without hesitating, the response she learned last Sunday, and turns to Jack and takes his hand in both of hers and just holds it.

At Communion Gus Ferreira brings the organ down to almost nothing, and the choir starts the Taizé chant that goes round and round, *Ubi caritas et amor*, and the ushers come up the side aisle a pew at a time. When it’s their pew Skye stands and steps out into the aisle to let him by, and he goes.
This week nobody passes the plate over him.

The line moves at its usual crawl, a man in front of him with a toddler asleep on his shoulder, a girl in a Marisol rowing jacket behind. On the way up he goes back over last night once, honestly, as they taught him for his First Communion, and comes out where she left him: at the bottom of the bluff stairs, with her fingers over his mouth and nothing gone anywhere. Osei is at the head of the center aisle with the ciborium. Jack opens his hands.
“The Body of Christ.”
“Amen.”

He has done this since he was seven, in Danny’s old shoes with Kleenex in the toes, and every time it is the same and it is never the same. He steps to the side and receives, and crosses himself, and turns back down the aisle with his hands folded, and the peace comes up in him that he has never been able to account for and has given up trying to.
When he gets back to the pew she’s kneeling.

Last Sunday she sat through all of it with her back straight and her hands in her lap, a guest at somebody else’s dinner. Today her hands are together on the back of the pew in front, and she doesn’t look at him as he slides in past her. She is looking at the altar like Nonna looks at her stove: hard, memorizing where everything is, so she could find it again in the dark.
He kneels beside her, close enough that their shoulders touch through the wool, and feels her breath catch once against his arm, and steady.
At the door after the recessional Osei is shaking hands in the sun with his stole still on, the late crowd going past him down the steps into the courtyard. He takes Skye’s hand first.
“Skye.”
“Father.”

He keeps her hand while he looks at Jack. The look is not gentle, and not soft, and it lasts about as long as a handshake. He doesn’t say anything. He lets go of her hand and turns to the family behind them.

Mrs. Fitch is at the foot of the steps in her good coat with a foil-covered sheet pan in both arms, on her way to the courtyard. She stops in front of Skye. “Lemon bars are *Sunday*,” she tells her, as if Skye had suggested otherwise, and goes on.
“I didn’t say anything,” Skye says.
“She knows.”
Skye takes his arm on the steps. The stone is warm under the sun, and the bells haven’t started yet, and she looks up at him in Ma’s tie. “Feed me,” she says.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything.
