s15a.slug: SUNDAY · 12:45 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE COUNTER
body: By daylight the Anchor is somebody else’s diner. The harbor comes in white through the front windows and finds every scratch in the counter, the booths are full of fishermen’s families in church clothes and a softball team in a winning mood, and Gloria is behind the register on a Sunday noon, which happens about as often as Easter, because the day girl is having a baby in Ventura. Rudy is on the line for the same baby. His transistor is on the shelf over the pass, turned low to a man selling tires in Spanish, and the rosary inked around his left wrist goes in and out of the steam.
Gloria has two coffees down before they’re all the way onto their stools, and looks at Skye, at the pinned-up hair and the buttons done to the throat, with the pencil going behind her ear.
“My granddaughter made me watch your program,” she says. “The Thursday one. With the lake.”
“I’m so sorry,” Skye says.
“Don’t be sorry, hon. Be smarter. That girl of yours should’ve left that boy in the second season. He’s got no chin, and he lies to her in a canoe.”
Skye sets down her coffee. “I *said* that. At the table read. I said Cassidy would push him out of the canoe and row back by herself. They gave the line to the lake.”

Gloria nods slowly, as if this confirms something she has long suspected about the lake. “Nights in here you were boysenberry,” she says. “I remember.” She looks again, with the harbor light full on Skye’s face. “Daytime you’re a different pie. Peach. Peach in January.” She writes on her pad without asking what they want. “You don’t believe it’s real, and there it is on the plate.”
She goes. Skye turns on her stool. “Is that good? Tell me that’s good.”
“She told me lattice-top. Pretty on top, everything leaking underneath.”
“So she’s met you.”

The peach comes out of a can under a lattice, warm, with the ice cream already giving up on top of it, and Gloria stands at the end of the counter with her arms folded until Skye has had the first bite and said so. Over it Skye tells him Corinne called during the Gospel. The network has two seats at a thing tonight, a Grammy party, and Corinne had a dress in mind and a reason it would help.
“I said I had church,” Skye says.
“Church was this morning.”
“I didn’t say which.” She cuts the point off her slice with the side of her fork. “She said, *You’ve been.* I said, *I’m going again.*”
She puts the point on his plate.

On Glenwood Avenue the point is the best bite, and there has been no peace at that table over who gets it since Nonna was a bride. She has given it away without looking up, the way you’d pass somebody the salt, and gone on talking about Corinne’s dress, and he eats the point of a canned-peach pie as slowly as a man can eat anything.
At the pass Rudy sets down a second slice, on the house, and slides it along the steel to her, and goes back to his tires without a word. Skye turns around to look at him.
“He likes you,” Gloria says, going by with the pot. “Don’t make a thing of it.”

At two o’clock the lot behind the Anchor is hot and smells of fish scales and asphalt, and the Saab has been sitting in the sun with its top down. Skye gets in behind the wheel and shrugs out of the gray wool and drops it on the back seat, and then she is in the white blouse with the sleeves pushed up, putting on her sunglasses. She looks at him over the top of them.
“Tonight,” she says.
He’s standing in the lot with his hands in his pockets and Ma’s tie pulled loose at his collar.
“Tonight.”

s15b.slug: SUNDAY · 12:40 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE OLIVE-TREE COURTYARD — COFFEE HOUR
body: Coffee hour happens under the olive trees whenever it isn’t raining, and it isn’t, so the courtyard is full: two card tables, an urn of coffee that tastes of the urn, the late crowd standing around in its good shoes, children going in circles around the fountain with powdered sugar on their mouths. Mrs. Fitch has the end of the second table with the foil off and the lemon bars cut in exact squares. She puts one on a napkin and holds it out to Skye.
“Thank you,” Skye says.
“Mm,” says Mrs. Fitch, and watches her eat it.

Tyler Brandt finds them by the fountain with a manila folder under his arm. “Brother,” he says to Jack, and to Skye, “Miss Callender. Mrs. Fitch says a novena requires the consent of the subject. I took it up with Father. Father said Mrs. Fitch is right, as a rule.” He opens the folder. “So I drew something up.”

body.title: ST. BRENDAN’S NEWMAN CENTER — NOVENA: CONSENT OF THE SUBJECT
body.text:
I, the undersigned, consent to be prayed for by Tyler Brandt (and anybody he can get) for nine (9) consecutive days, beginning Monday, February 1, 2010, for the following intention: *the pair of you.* I understand that I may withdraw my consent at any time, and that it will not stop him.

Signature of subject: ______________
Witness: ______________

body: Skye reads it to the bottom with her lips pressed together. “What’s my billing?”
“Ma’am?”
“Is it the pair of us, or the pair of you? Am I above the line?”
Tyler looks at the form with real concern. “It’s — alphabetical? To God?”
“Callender,” Skye says to Jack. “I go first.”
“Do I sign too?” Jack says.
“You’re covered, Brother. You’re Catholic.”

Tyler holds out a pen. Skye props the folder on the edge of the fountain and signs on the line, fast, with a flourish: *Skye*, the big loop under it running out past the margin, the same autograph she has put on ten thousand eight-by-tens. Then she turns, and holds the pen out to Mrs. Fitch for the witness line.

Mrs. Fitch accepts the pen after a moment and writes *D. Fitch* under the loop in the hand that does the bulletin, small and upright, and hands the pen back to Tyler without a word, and Tyler holds the form against his chest like a diploma, and Jack has to turn around and look at the fountain until his face is his own again.

Across the courtyard Becca Lindell is holding somebody’s baby by the bench around the big olive. She sees Jack, and lifts the baby’s fist and waves it at him, and then her own hand, and goes back to the baby.
Under the far tree Father Osei is out of his vestments with a paper cup, listening to an old man in a Korea veterans cap. He sees them. He doesn’t come over.
“Corinne called during the Gospel,” Skye says, with the second lemon bar. “The network has two seats at a Grammy party tonight. She had a dress in mind and a reason it would help.”
“What’d you tell her?”
“I said I had church.” She licks sugar off her thumb. “She said, *Church is in the morning.* I said I have a lot of church.”

At two o’clock the bells go for nothing in particular and the courtyard empties out toward the lot. The Saab has been sitting in the sun at the far end of it with its top down. Skye gets in behind the wheel and pushes her sunglasses up into her pinned hair, and Jack stands at the open passenger door with one hand on the top of it. He’s walking up the hill; she’s going home to learn lines.
“Tonight,” he says.
She looks at him from behind the wheel, buttoned to the throat for Mass.
“Tonight.”

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 4:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — GLENWOOD
body: A wrist corsage lies on the third step down, white, browned at the edges of the petals, left over from somebody’s Saturday. The four o’clock sun comes through the wired glass at the turn of the stairs and lays a grid across it. Jack steps over it and sits on the top landing with the RAZR open on his knee, because on Ma’s Sundays the call comes after the dishes, and the east stairwell is where Delgado keeps its bars. Down the shaft somebody drags a garment bag along a floor, a door goes, a girl laughs in a hallway at something that happened last night: the building on the afternoon after a formal.
It rings, and the little outside screen says GLENWOOD.
“Did you eat?” Ma says. “Don’t lie to me, I can hear it in your voice.”

body.text: “Pie, Ma. At the Anchor.”
“Pie isn’t eating.”

body: Behind her the faucet runs, and a pan goes into the rack. “Father Dom did Nazareth at the 8:00,” she says. “A prophet’s never welcome at home. Four minutes. He was good.”
“Father Osei had that one this morning.”
“It’s the Gospel, Jackie. They don’t change it for California.” The faucet goes off. “Your father said *that’s for sure*. In the pew. Out loud.”
“Pop did?”
“Rita Pallante turned around. He looked at her till she turned back.”
Jack leans his head back against the cinderblock. In the wired glass the sun has slid down a row of the wire.
“He came in with me after, to Danny. He told him the Browns are keeping Mangini. Again. Danny put his head down on the table and said bad news is what the mail is for.”
“Ma —”

“It’s Catholic Schools Week, so there were donuts in the hall, and Rita cornered me at the donuts. Was she Catholic. I said she’s baptized. Rita said that isn’t the same thing. I said, *Rita, it’s a start.*” “Your father looked at the picture over my shoulder and said *that’s a lot of limes*. Then he went to the garage.”
“It was a taquería, Ma.”
“I looked a long time. She’s tiny.”
“Ma.”
“I’m not saying anything. I’m saying somebody should feed her. It says one-thirty in the morning.”
“It had a heat lamp.”
“I saw the lamp. Rosie wants to know where the crab was.”
“Tell Rosie the crab sends his regards.”

“I’m not telling her that. She’ll want to write him. Nonna’s been saying *Maria Caterina* since the 8:00. She lit another one. That’s two. Father Dom says the candle box needs a refill, and he’s not saying whose fault.”
On Glenwood Avenue the chair scrapes back. Ma says *Gina, I’m not finished*, and Gina says *you’re finished, you’re so finished*, and the phone changes size in somebody’s hand.
“Jack. It’s me. I told him. I waited till he’d had the honey bun, like you said.”
“Good.”
“I said *Mary Catherine* and he said *a NUN?* Like that. Loud. Then I told him about the picture. The lamp, the limes, your face. I did your face.”
“I don’t have a face.”
“You have *the* face. He made me do it twice. He said *oh, he’s gone.* And then he said — hold on, I have to do his voice — *ask her what she lost the bet for.*”
“What bet?”
“That’s what Ma said! He says you tricked her somehow, it’s the only explanation, and he wants to know how.”
“Tell him I didn’t trick her.”
“He said you’d say that. He said *that’s what a guy who tricked her would say.*”
Jack laughs, and Gina waits for him, drumming something on the table.

“And then he laughed so hard the CO came over. The big one, Jack. Ma put her hand over her eyes. The CO stood there with his newspaper, and Danny said *sorry, sir, family news*, and the CO went back. And Ma said happy birthday early, from all of us, in case your card’s late, and he said late’s a Costigan tradition. Okay. Here. Ma’s reaching.”
“Jackie.”

He hears her take a breath, the Tuesday one, from the bottom of her, and a dish towel come down on the counter. Nothing comes after it. The line holds the faucet and Nonna’s beads in the next room, and it goes on holding them past where a call ought to stop.
“Did you go up today?”

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’ Sunday, after the 8:00 and Trumbull: Father Dom said a prophet’s never welcome at home, and Pop said that’s for sure in the pew. She’d seen the taco picture: *she’s tiny.* Then one question — did I go up today. I said yes. She said good.

choices.text: “I went up, Ma. With her there.”
response: “With her there,” Ma says, trying it. “Did she stay in the pew?”
“She knelt, Ma.”
“Good.” It comes out of her on a long breath, all the way down.
Through the wall Nonna goes on with the decade, and drops the name into it again, *Maria Caterina*, at the end of every Hail Mary, like a bell.

choices.text: “Tell Nonna thank you. For the candle.”
response: “Yes, Ma,” he says. “And tell Nonna thank you. For the candle.”
Ma tells her, with her hand nowhere near the phone: “Mamma, Jackie says thank you for the candle.” From the front room Nonna answers with something short in dialect, and Ma does not translate it.
“Good,” Ma says, about all of it.

choices.text: “Yes, Ma.”
response: “Good.” It comes out of her a half-step higher than anything she has said yet.
The faucet comes on again. “Eat something real,” Ma says over it, and then there is only the water.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 9:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, UPSTAIRS — THE TUB
body: The bath is already run when he gets to the top of the stairs. The bathroom door stands open, and the only light in there is two candles — one on the sill of the open window, one on the floor by the tub’s back foot — and past them the moon coming up over the roofs, still full, or near enough, white across the old tile, black and white hexagons, half of them cracked since before Sol was born. The tub stands in the middle of the floor on four iron claws, deep and white and steaming. Her iPod sits on the edge of the sink in a speaker no bigger than a paperback, turned low: a harpsichord picking its way down over a drum as slow as a pulse, and a woman’s voice somewhere far inside it, too far in to make out a word.
The only other clawfoot Jack has ever known stands on its end in the side yard on Glenwood, painted blue inside, with the Blessed Mother in it and Nonna’s geraniums at her feet.

Skye is in the doorway in a white towel, her hair twisted up off her neck with a pencil stuck through it to hold it. Before he’s off the last stair she puts her hand on his chest, the fingers spread over his sweatshirt, over his heart, and keeps it there, and looks up at him, and says it.
“I watched you go up,” she says. “I kept my word all week. So I’m asking. I want to have sex with you. Tonight. I wanted you to hear it before anything, so you’d know it isn’t the bath talking.”

body.text: “You got there first on Wednesday,” she says. “I’m getting *this* first.”
body.else: “I’m going first this time,” she says.

body: “I heard you,” he says. It isn’t a yes, and it isn’t the other thing, and she nods as if it’s the answer she expected. Her hand stays where it is, and his heart goes on telling it whatever it’s telling it, and she lets it talk as long as it wants.
He looks at her in the candlelight with her chin up and her hand on his heart, and he loves her. It sits in his chest as plain as weather.

She takes the hand back. She lets the towel go onto the bathmat like a towel, steps over the high white side into the water, and sits down in it to her shoulders. “Get in, Youngstown. That’s my second bath. The first one went cold while I practiced.”

He gets out of his clothes by the sink with his back to the mirror — the sweatshirt, the T-shirt, the jeans he wore to Mass with the bulletin still folded in the back pocket — and there’s nothing to it. It’s a bath.
When he steps in and sits down behind her, the water climbs to within a finger of the rim and stops there, trembling, and the two of them hold very still and watch it.
“Archimedes,” she says, not moving.
“He ran down the street after. Naked. Yelling.”
“Del Playa’s seen worse. Don’t tempt me.”

The water is hot enough to sting. The porcelain where it rises out of the water behind him is cold as a church step, and she settles back against his chest between his knees with a long, contented noise, her pinned-up hair against his cheek and the knobs of her spine against his breastbone one at a time. He grew up in a house with one bathroom and two sisters, and nobody in it ever ran him a bath.

“Me first,” she says. She takes his right hand out of the water and puts it on her breast, and takes his left and puts it under the water between her thighs, and holds both of them there under her own. “Like that. Slow. Slower than that — like you’ve got all night. You’ve got all night.”

He does what she tells him. She’s specific about it, low against his jaw — *there*, and *lighter*, and *don’t get clever, just that, keep doing just that* — and after a little she takes her own hands away and leaves it to him. By now he has the rest of it by heart: where her breath catches and what it does when it catches, the way her heel comes up out of the water to hunt for the rim, the moment to change nothing at all. Her weight is all on him, slippery and warm, and every time she breathes he feels it the length of his own chest. The water rocks with her. It laps up the sides and over, and the candle on the floor leans and gutters in the wash, and she pushes back hard against him and comes with her head thrown back on his shoulder and her mouth open at his ear, and a wave of bathwater goes over the rim and across the tile.
When the water settles she says it breathless, against his jaw. “Look at you. You used to be terrible at this.”
She turns her head on his shoulder until her mouth is at his ear. “Your turn. Out loud.”

choices.text: *Tell her exactly what you want. The whole sentence.*
response: So he tells her, start to finish, with his eyes on hers in the candlelight and nothing mumbled to the ceiling: he wants her mouth on him. Here, in the water. Slowly. And he wants to watch her do it.
Skye lifts her head off his shoulder to look at him. “Again,” she says. “The part about watching.”

He says it again. She listens to it like music she paid for. She turns in the water, slopping half the bath onto the floor, and kneels up between his knees with the candlelight on her wet shoulders, and takes him in her hand, and then in her mouth, slowly, her eyes on his face and not leaving it. The rim of the tub is under both his hands before he knows he’s reached for it. The harpsichord goes on picking its way down. She takes the time he asked for and more, until his head is back against the porcelain and her name is coming out of him in pieces — and then, on purpose, short of the end, she stops, and comes up, and wipes her mouth with the back of her wrist.
“Not in here,” she says. “I want the bed for that.”

She stands up out of the bath, and that’s when they find out the water has gone cold. She shivers from her knees to her shoulders and says something about it that would get her fired off *Sweetwater*.

choices.text: *Ask her to stand up and let you look at her.*
response: “Stand up,” he says. “Let me look at you.”

She stands up in the tub with the water running off her. In the candlelight she sets her hands on her hips and her chin up, and waits. He looks as long as he wants, and he tells her what he sees. Not the pose. The water running down the middle of her and pooling in her navel. The gooseflesh coming up along her arms in the air off the window, and her nipples drawn tight with it. The pink line the rim of the tub left across the small of her back. The pencil in her hair, gone crooked, about to fall. A freckle on her hip he has never seen before. Somewhere around the freckle her hands come down off her hips and hang at her sides, and she quits posing and just stands there in the draft from the window and lets him.

He sits up in the water and puts his mouth on her where she stands, his hands on the backs of her thighs to keep her there. She gets one hand in his wet hair. The other goes out and finds the wall, the tile above the soap dish, and braces there, and her knees start to go, and he doesn’t let them; he holds her up and keeps on until she comes with her cheek almost to the tile and his name coming back off it.
When he sinks down again the water closes over him cold — it’s been cold for some time — and she’s shaking.

choices.text: *Ask for the thing you’ve been thinking about since Monday.*
response: “Monday,” he says. “Your mattress. You on top of me with my wrists in your hand, not letting me move.” He keeps his eyes on hers for the rest. “I’ve thought about it every day since. In the Commons. At the Anchor, holding a pie.”

She laughs, low, from the back of her throat. She turns over in the water and kneels up between his knees, takes both his wrists in one hand and lifts them over his head to the high back of the tub, and pins them there against the cold porcelain. Her other hand goes under the water. “Don’t move,” she says into his ear, and he doesn’t, and she takes him in her fist under the water, slow and then not slow, her breasts slick against his chest and her mouth at his ear telling him exactly how still he’s being, how good he is at it, how much longer he’s going to have to be, and the bath goes over the rim in a wave and drowns the candle on the floor with a hiss. He pulls at her grip without meaning to. She tightens it and doesn’t stop —
— and stops. Lets go of his wrists. Sits back on her heels in water he only now notices has gone as cold as the Channel.
“Bed,” she says. “Now. You’re turning blue.”

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 10:30 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE NO
body: Her bed is the mattress on the floor under the open window, and the moon comes in over the sill and off the white wall onto the sheet, enough to see by and no more.

body.text: She finishes what she started in the tub. She’s unhurried about it now, kneeling over him in the light off the wall with her hair coming down out of the pencil around her face, no water to fight and nothing to brace against, and she makes it last. When he comes it’s with her name in his mouth — both of her names, *Skye* and then the other one, the one from the taquería, never said in a bed before now. She goes still. Then she puts her face down on his stomach and says it too, the whole thing, every syllable, into his skin, like a title she’s won.

It’s her turn to look. She puts him on his back in the light off the wall and kneels beside him and takes as long as he did — longer — and doesn’t tell him one thing she sees, and he finds out from the other side what that costs. Then her mouth on him, unhurried, with her hand spread low on his stomach to keep him down on the sheet, until he comes under it, her name breaking in the middle on the way out of him.

She puts him on his back and lays his hands flat on the mattress on either side of his head, and lets go of them. “You keep them there,” she says. “I’m not doing it for you this time.” Then her mouth: his throat, the notch of his collarbone, a slow line down the middle of him, her tongue at his navel, her wet hair dragging cold behind it over his chest, and then she takes him into her mouth, unhurried, with her eyes up on his face to see if his hands have moved. They haven’t. His fingers are dug into the sheet to the knuckle. He tells her, in a voice he doesn’t recognize, that he can’t, and she lifts her head just long enough to say *yes, you can*, and he does. He keeps them there through all of it, the heat and the slow pull of her and her hand closed at the base of him, until he comes with his back up off the mattress and both fists full of sheet and her name torn in half on the way out.

body: After that there’s no order to it and no hurry, and nobody’s turn. They trade, out loud now, both of them. “Turn over,” he says, and she does, and he puts his mouth to the small of her back and works down from there, the backs of her thighs, the crease behind one knee, telling her low where he’s going a sentence before he gets there, so she has to wait for it. She makes him do the whole length of her like that. “Now you,” she says, when he’s back up beside her on the pillow. “Your hand. Slower than that. And don’t you look at the ceiling. Look at me.” He looks at her. He asks for hers on him at the same time, and gets it, and for a long while the two of them lie face to face on one pillow, working each other slowly with their eyes open, and neither of them looks away.

body.text: Then she does a thing he would never have known to ask for. She lies back with her knees up in the light off the wall and puts her own hand between her legs, and tells him to watch, and to say what he sees, the way he did in the bath. So he does — her stomach drawing tight, the color climbing her throat, her free hand finding his wrist and gripping it — and she comes slow and long and nearly quiet with his voice going on at her ear, rolling up through her, her heel pushing at the sheet.
body.else: Then he goes down on her in the light off the wall with her knees up and her fingers in his hair, and this time she hardly directs him at all; now and then she says his name, low, to check he’s still there. When she comes it’s slow and long and nearly quiet, rolling up through her, her heel on his shoulder and her stomach trembling under his hand.

body: Somewhere in there he finds the pencil, under his back, and she takes it out of his hand and throws it at the window.

Later — he couldn’t say how much later; the moon has gone some way along the wall — she’s over him. Her knees on either side of his hips. Her hands on his chest. Her hair all the way down now. Nothing on either of them, anywhere. She lowers herself along him until she’s lying on him from hip to breast, and there’s no air left between their bodies but in one place, and he can feel that one place exactly: the wet heat of her right there, a breath away from where all of him is straining up toward it, so near it’s hardly a distance at all. They’ve never been this close. Above him she has gone completely still. His hands are on her hips, his fingers spread over the bones of them, and they’re what’s holding it — his own two hands, keeping the last inch where it is while every other part of him argues with them. His forearms are shaking. Her breasts are against his chest and her heartbeat is going into him through them, fast, and the light off the wall is in her loosened hair, and he can feel how little it would take — not a decision, hardly a motion, just his hands opening.
She’s breathing hard. She puts her mouth beside his ear.
“Jack,” she says, into his ear, with her eyes shut. That’s all. She asked at the top of the stairs.

He doesn’t say anything. The surf comes up through the window and goes out again. A car goes by on Del Playa with its windows down and takes its radio with it. Her breath is on his neck, fast and then slower. Under his hands the long muscles of her hips tremble with holding still, and his hands don’t move.
In the silence he sees the aisle this morning: the walk back from the altar with the taste still in his mouth, and her in the pew ahead of him on her knees, not looking at him, looking at the altar.
“It’s still no,” he says. “For now.”
She goes on breathing against his neck. He knows how that sounds, and he won’t sand it, so he says the rest.
“But it’s closer than it’s ever been.”

She lifts her head to look at him, her face just over his in the moonlight off the wall, close enough that he can see her eyes go from one of his to the other. He has one reason left, and she’s owed that too.

body.text: “This morning,” she says. “That’s what’s holding it.” She counts something on his chest with one finger. He’d bet it’s the days to next Sunday.
“You said all that,” she says into his collarbone, “and then you said no.” She lifts her head. She’s smiling.
“You bit me back,” she says. “That’s new.” She touches her lip.

body: “That was a no,” she says. “I heard it. It just had its car keys out.”
She tries his line in her own mouth, slowly, to hear what it sounds like there. “*Closer than it’s ever been.*” She doesn’t get off him.
“Love is patient,” she says. “A girl in a navy skirt read it at me this morning. So now it’s official.”
“She read it at everybody.”
“She was looking at me.”
“Everybody looks at you.”
“Not like that. Like she was reading me my lines.” She leans down until her nose is against his and her eyes are too close to focus on. “I liked them,” she says. “I’m keeping them.”
“So,” she says. “What does the letter say?”
He tells her. It doesn’t take long, and she listens to all of it with her nose against his, and when he’s done she nods, once, like a woman reading a contract she has decided to sign.

She keeps the letter. She stays where she is, astride him, and his hands stay where they are, and the distance he named stays exactly what it was — and inside it she starts to move. Against him, never onto him: slow at first, the long slide of her along him and back, wet and hot and maddeningly patient, her palms spread on his chest and her eyes open on his, finding out how much there is to do in the room he’s left her. There’s a great deal. He finds that out too. She rocks and he rises to meet her and his hands hold and hold, his wrists aching with it and his fingers sunk in the give of her hips, and she starts to say something in Corinne’s vowels and loses it halfway, and then it isn’t slow. The sheet is gone somewhere off the end of the mattress. The damp has come up at her temples, and then she bends to him and her hair falls around both their faces and closes them in, and in the dark of it they breathe each other’s breath, mouths open and not kissing, until she comes with a sound into his mouth and he goes with her, between them, against her stomach, never inside her, the two of them shaking together, his hands still on her hips and still holding.

Afterward they come apart. She slides off him onto her side and lies with her knee over his and her heart still going against his arm. While they weren’t looking the moon has come down off the wall, and it lies on the floorboards now among their clothes.

s18b.slug: SUNDAY · 11:45 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE QUESTION
body: It’s as dark in the room as it gets with the window open on Del Playa: the moon on the floor, a streetlight down at the corner, the white of the sheet. The lamp is off. The candles in the bathroom have burned down or drowned; he can’t smell them anymore. She’s lying on his chest with her ear over his heart, drawing something on his ribs with one fingernail. He’s decided it’s the state of Ohio. It turns out, when he asks, to be a horse.
“Gina was telling your brother today,” she says. “You said. What did he say?”
“Gina told him across the table,” he says, and feels her go still to listen. “He said, *a NUN?*”

Skye laughs so hard she has to roll off him and put her face in the pillow to keep it off the street. When he gets to the CO coming over she comes up for air, and when he gets to the bet — Danny wants to know what she lost it for — she goes back in.
She comes up out of the pillow wiping her eyes with the heel of her hand. “What *did* I lose the bet for?”
“He wants to know.”
“Tell him I’m still deciding.” She settles back down on him, her cheek on his chest again. “I like your brother.”
“He thinks I must’ve tricked you somehow.”
“Into what?”
“Any of it.”
She thinks that over with her chin on his breastbone. “Tell him it was the flannel,” she says.

She’s quiet after that, her ear back over his heart, long enough that he thinks she’s gone to sleep. “It’s slow now,” she says at last, about the heart. “It was very fast before. I was keeping track.” The fingernail goes back to the horse. The surf comes up through the window, and a gust off the water lifts the curtain and lets it down.
“What was the question?” she says. “The one I’m the answer to.”
She doesn’t lift her head. The fingernail has stopped on his ribs, wherever the horse’s heart would be.
He gives her Nonna’s.
“She asked me what makes me pray.”
The fingernail doesn’t move.
“Do I?”
“Yes.”

It’s true. He prays for her at red lights, in the space between the red and the green. He has prayed for her by name. And this morning on his knees beside her, with the Host still on his tongue, he said her name again — both of them, now.
“What do you say?” she says. “When you do it. For me.”
“A Hail Mary. Your name. Then whatever I want for you that day.”
“Like what?”
“That you sleep. That your mother calls less.” He thinks about it. “That Corinne gets a cold.”
Her head comes up. “You pray for Corinne to get a cold.”
“A small one. Over a weekend.”
She puts her head back down, and he feels her smile against his chest, and then he feels it go.
“You’re going Wednesday,” she says.
“Yes.”
“And you have to tell him you won’t do it again. That’s the rule. The purpose part.” She waits until he says yes to that too. “And then you come back here.”
“Yes.”

“I’m not mad at it.” She says it fast. “I want you to know that. I came to your Mass. I knelt. I’d do it again next Sunday, I’d do it every Sunday, I liked it, I liked watching you go up. That isn’t the part.”
She comes up on one elbow, and he can see the shine of her eyes in the dark and not much else.
“So here’s mine,” she says. “When it’s yes —”
*When*, she says, and he doesn’t correct her.

“— am I only ever going to be something you carry into that little room on a Wednesday?” Her voice doesn’t go up at the end. “You go in and say me to a man behind a screen, and he tells you what I cost, and you come out, and you get to go up on Sunday. And I’m still here. I’m always still here.”

body.text: “I can live in the daylight column,” she says. “I told you I could. But this isn’t daylight, Jack. I’ll be in the bad column on a Wednesday every week of my life with you.”
body.else: “I’ll be the thing you tell him about on a Wednesday,” she says. “Every week of my life with you.”

body: She’s quiet. Her heart is going against his ribs, fast for somebody lying still.

“Monday I didn’t finish something,” she says. “I said I didn’t want to be the occasion. I had the rest of it right there, and I put it back, because it wasn’t ready.” She takes a breath. “It’s ready.”
“I want to be the good thing,” she says. “With the lights off.”
The lights are off.

There’s one answer in him. It has a priest in it, and a Wednesday, and a church she knelt in this morning for his sake and may only be visiting. He can’t put that in her hands at midnight in the dark with nothing on and call it an answer. She’s waiting. He can hear the surf, and her breathing, and his own heart under her ear, and none of it is going to say anything for him.

She puts her head back down on his chest. After a moment, smaller, into his skin: “I mean it about fast.”
And later, when he thinks she’s asleep: “Anybody else I know would’ve had an answer. A good one. I’d have believed it for a week.”

“That was a good one,” she says, with her back to him. “I’m going to need a better one.”

body: She walks him down. She goes ahead of him on the stairs in his flannel and nothing else, buttoned wrong, past Tomás’s dark door and across the front room and out onto the porch, and at the top step she stops with one hand on the post. Sol’s swing is moving a little on its new chains in the wind off the water.

body.text: “Like last time,” she says, and pulls the flannel together at her throat. “I liked last time. Go before I quit liking it.”
body.else: “Go home, Youngstown,” she says, and pulls the flannel together at her throat. “Before I change my mind about letting you.”

body: He goes down the steps. When he looks back from the street she’s still up there, a pale shape in the dark of the porch with the flannel pulled shut.

He goes up Del Playa with his hands in the pocket of his sweatshirt — a couch on somebody’s lawn, a porch light left burning, a cooler tipped over in the gutter, the surf under the bluff louder than it ever is by day — and turns onto Ocean Road. St. Brendan’s is dark on the hill, the bell tower black against a sky the moon has washed almost white, the doors shut on the place where he knelt this morning. He knows it’s there without looking.
Under a streetlight on Ocean Road he opens the RAZR. Three he never heard: one from before midnight, two from after one.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer. She saw my face from across the room and asked twice, and walked me out past the host and down Sunset to the ocean, making me explain myself the whole way and telling me why I’m wrong. She’s a union member. Two of them. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she told me about her father: Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name out loud. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. She asked before she posted us. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I went home. She walked me to the top step.

s19s.slug: MONDAY · 12:55 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: He stays.

He lies on his back in her bed with nothing on either of them and her asleep against him, and sleep is all it is; he keeps it to that. Her knee is over his. Her hand is open on his chest where it fell, and now and then the fingers move a little, still drawing horses. The moon has gone off the floor, and the window is full of it instead, and the curtain lifts in the air off the water and settles again. He isn’t tired at all.
He says a Hail Mary for her under his breath, the red-light kind, fast, with her name on the end of it. And another, slower, for Danny, whose birthday is Tuesday.
She stirs. She doesn’t open her eyes. Into his shoulder, half asleep, she says, “Mary Catherine says goodnight.”
“Goodnight,” he tells her. Both of them.
She smiles without waking, or he thinks she does; in the dark he can’t be sure of anything but the weight of her, and the warmth, and her breath going slow against his collarbone.

On the floor by the mattress his jeans buzz against the boards. He reaches down one-armed without waking her, fishes the RAZR out of the pocket, and opens it low against his chest so the screen won’t find her face. One from before midnight he never heard, and two just now.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer. She saw my face from across the room and asked twice, and walked me out past the host and down Sunset to the ocean, making me explain myself the whole way and telling me why I’m wrong. She’s a union member. Two of them. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she told me about her father: Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name out loud. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. She asked before she posted us. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep.
